##### An Improved Conjecturing Algorithm for the Diversity Issue.

Suppose $`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ is the final prover
trained by a self-play algorithm like
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Whereas
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
under
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
provides guarantees of
$`|K^{p}(f)|:=|\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\}|`$, the size of
the prover’s knowledge,
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
does not guarantee the diversity of the prover’s knowledge. For
hyperparameter $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, we study how to optimize a proxy
for diversity of the prover’s knowledge,
$`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f)|:=|\{x^{\prime}\in V:\exists x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\textup{ and }\textup{dist}(x,x^{\prime})\leq\tau\}|`$.
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In A Baseline Conjecturing Algorithm. ‣ 1.1 Technical Overview ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
depicts two provers, $`f_{1}`$ and $`f_{2}`$, that both can prove the
same number of theorems ($`|K^{p}(f_{1})|=|K^{p}(f_{2})|`$), but where
$`f_{1}`$’s knowledge set is much less diverse, in the sense that
$`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f_{1})|\ll|K^{p}_{\tau}(f_{2})|`$.

Suppose prover $`f`$ is trained on theorem distribution
$`D\in\Delta(V)`$ in the sense that
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$
(as in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
[Lemma 5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 5.3 (Large "Div"^𝑃*𝜏 implies large 𝐾^𝑝*𝜏). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that in order to maximize $`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f)|`$, it is reasonable
to maximize the following property of $`f`$’s training distribution:
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D):=\frac{1}{||D^{\top}P^{\tau}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{x\in V}(D^{\top}P^{\tau}e_{x})^{2}\frac{1}{\pi(x)}}`$,
where $`P`$ is the transition matrix of a reversible, nearest-neighbor
Markov chain. With this observation, the goal is to design a
conjecturing algorithm that generates training distributions
$`\{D_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ where $`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t})`$
is large for each $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$. We propose
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
an improved conjecturer that defines a push-forward map
$`C:V\to\Delta(V)`$ where $`\forall x\in V`$, $`C(x)\in\Delta(N(x))`$.
The weighting of $`C(x)`$ is determined by maximizing
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(C(x))`$.

|     |                                        |                                                                                                                                                                              |     |       |
| --- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\forall x\in V,\,C(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\max_{\mu\in\Delta(N(x))}\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(\mu)=\arg\min_{\mu\in\Delta(N(x))}\mu^{\top}P^{\tau}\textup{diag}(1/\pi)(P^{\tau})^{\top}\mu`$ |     | (1.2) |

[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
needs to compute the diffusion similarity
$`\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,y^{\prime}):=e_{y}^{\top}P^{\tau}\textup{diag}(1/\pi)(P^{\tau})^{\top}e_{y^{\prime}}`$
for every pair of neighbors $`y,y^{\prime}\in N(x)`$ of $`x`$. ¹¹ 1 To
further motivate diffusion similarity, note it is closely related to
diffusion distance, used for graph partitioning [Lafon and Lee
(2006)](#bib.bib40). We show the diffusion similarity can be computed by
embedding each node in $`G`$ into Euclidean space via an embedding model
learned with contrastive learning, and then computing the inner product
between embeddings. This can be used as a subroutine in a conjecturing
algorithm like
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Theorem 1.2.

([Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
Informal) Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be an undirected, connected theorem graph. Let
$`\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(|V|)}`$ be the class of all mappings from $`V`$ to
$`\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$, and
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\subset\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(|V|)}`$ a class of
embedding models. For any $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$,
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}^{\tau}:\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(|V|)}\to\mathbb{R}`$
is a contrastive loss with time-scale parameter $`\tau`$
([Equation 3.1](#S3.E1 "In Contrastive Learning. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
Assume $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ contains a global minimizer of
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}^{\tau}(\cdot)`$. For any such global
minimizer $`h_{\theta_{*}}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$, then
$`\forall u,v\in V,\;\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(u,v)=h_{\theta_{*}}(u)^{\top}h_{\theta_{*}}(v)`$.

Under additional assumptions, we prove
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
which is an extension to the result of
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
that applies for classes of embedding models
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ where models
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\ni h_{\theta}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ have
small embedding dimension $`k\ll|V|`$.
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
provides approximation-guarantees for an embedding model that is learned
via empirical risk minimization (ERM).

In short, our contributions are:

1.  1.  We provide a theoretical framework for understanding and designing
        self-play theorem proving algorithms. The framework formalizes the
        set of theorems as a graph, where nodes are theorems. It introduces
        a set of primitive assumptions
        ([Assumption 1](#Thmassumption1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
        –
        [4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
        that describe the properties of the graph and the computational
        primitives available to a self-play algorithm.
2.  2.  We show in
        [Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
        that if the theorem graph and conjecturer satisfy a
        well-connectedness property
        ([Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
        the number of theorems the prover-conjecturer system
        ([Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
        proves grows exponentially with the number of self-play iterations.
3.  3.  Motivated by an issue encountered empirically by self-play
        algorithms where the conjecturer generates artificially complex and
        non-fundamental theorems, we propose a diversity measure for a
        training distribution of theorems generated by a conjecturer
        ([Definition 5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
        and an improved conjecturer
        ([Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
        that locally maximizes this diversity measure, by computing the
        diffusion similarity
        ([Definition 5.4](#S5.Thmtheorem4 "Definition 5.4. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
        between neighboring theorems in the theorem graph.
4.  4.  In
        [Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
        and
        [Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
        we describe a method to compute the diffusion similarity of two
        nodes of the theorem graph by using contrastive learning to embed
        nodes into Euclidean space and then computing the inner-product
        between the embeddings.

## 2 Related Work

##### LLM-Based Formal Theorem Proving Systems.

Formal theorem proving with LLMs in Lean [de Moura and Ullrich
(2021)](#bib.bib30) is commonly divided into two paradigms: step-level
interaction and whole-proof generation. Step-level methods interact with
Lean incrementally, proposing one tactic at a time [Achim and others
(2025)](#bib.bib16); [Hubert and others (2025)](#bib.bib17); [Wu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib18); [Xin and others (2025b)](#bib.bib19); [Xin et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib20). Whole-proof methods instead generate a complete
Lean proof in a single interaction [Chen and others (2025)](#bib.bib21);
[Ji et al. (2025)](#bib.bib22); [Lin et al. (2025)](#bib.bib23); [Lin
and others (2025)](#bib.bib24); [Xin and others (2025a)](#bib.bib28);
[Ren and others (2025)](#bib.bib25); [Shang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib26);
[Wang and others (2025)](#bib.bib27); [Zhou and others
(2025)](#bib.bib29).

##### Self-play for Formal Theorem Proving.

Regarding self-play theorem proving systems, STP instantiates a
prover-conjecturer self-play loop from pre-trained LLMs, where the
conjecturer is trained to generate synthetic theorems that are barely
provable by the current prover [Dong and Ma (2025)](#bib.bib10). Minimo
instantiates a prover-conjecturer self-play loop to learn a prover from
scratch, where the conjecturer generates conjectures via constrained
decoding and the prover guides an MCTS proof search [Poesia et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib14). In contrast to these empirical works, our work
develops a theoretical framework for analyzing when prover-conjecturer
self-play can expand the set of provable theorems.

##### Theoretical Analyses of Self-play Algorithms.

Existing theoretical analyses of self-play largely focus on adversarial
settings, such as zero-sum Markov games. The theorem-proving setting we
study is different: the prover and conjecturer have asymmetric but
cooperative roles. [Bai et al. (2020)](#bib.bib11) provide a theoretical
analysis of self-play algorithms in zero-sum Markov Games, showing
convergence to a Nash Equilibrium [Bai et al. (2020)](#bib.bib11). The
Wasserstein GAN training algorithm [Arjovsky et al. (2017)](#bib.bib33)
is a theoretically-grounded asymmetric self-play algorithm, but still
where the agents are adversarial to each other. Our work also differs
from works that study how to learn a model to verify theorems in a
purely statistical setting [Balcan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib32). Our
setting is non-statistical since the goal of the training algorithm is
to allow the final model to generalize beyond its starting distribution,
not just to generalize well on its starting distribution given i.i.d.
samples. However, we will assume some statistical-learning primitives
([Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
in our framework.

##### Theorem Graphs.

Prior works formalize the graph or hyper-graph structure of mathematical
theorems [Geuvers and Loeb (2006)](#bib.bib35); [Barkeshli et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib34). In [Geuvers and Loeb (2006)](#bib.bib35), each node
represents a statement; the statement corresponding to a node can be
deduced in one step via a deduction rule from the statements
corresponding to its descendants. [Barkeshli et al. (2026)](#bib.bib34)
formalizes nodes as statements, and each $`(p,q)`$ hyper-edge
corresponds to applying a deduction rule on $`p`$ input statements to
yield $`q`$ output conclusions. Axioms of the logical system are root
nodes. In relation to these works, our notion of a theorem graph still
represents mathematical statements as nodes. However, the definition of
an edge is not defined in terms of deduction rules in a particular
logical system. Rather, edges are determined by the class of prover
models $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, where an edge between two
theorems $`(x,y)`$ indicates that for every prover
$`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, the success rate of $`f`$ on
theorem $`x`$ is not too different from the success rate of $`f`$ on
theorem $`y`$.

##### Graph Exploration Algorithms, Graph Diffusion, Contrastive Learning.

Given a graph, the question of how to design an algorithm to explore the
graph efficiently has been studied in [Kim et al. (2025)](#bib.bib5).
They formalize chain-of-thought reasoning as a random walk over a graph
of ideas, where the goal of the reasoner is to hit a particular node of
the graph, starting at a designated start node. The underlying graphs
they study are metastable graphs [Bovier et al. (2002)](#bib.bib31). The
question we study in
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is conceptually related to [Kim et al. (2025)](#bib.bib5), in that we
want to find a graph algorithm that can efficiently explore a graph with
poor connectivity, such as metastable graphs. However, our proposed
graph-exploration algorithms are different from [Kim et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib5). In particular, our algorithm uses a similarity
measure between nodes in the graph, called the diffusion similarity,
that is defined in terms of a random walk on the graph. The diffusion
similarity measure is closely related to the diffusion distance, a graph
metric which is useful for characterizing the clustering-structure of a
graph [Coifman and Lafon (2006)](#bib.bib36). Finally, we propose a new
way to compute the diffusion similarity, using a version of contrastive
learning formalized by [HaoChen et al. (2022)](#bib.bib6), who provide a
theoretical characterization of the global minimizers of a particular
contrastive loss in terms of the minimizers of a related matrix
factorization objective.

## 3 Preliminaries

##### Notation.

$`0\in\mathbb{N}`$. $`[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}`$. For a set $`V`$,
$`2^{V}`$ is its power set. For $`v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}`$,
$`\textup{diag}(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}`$ is the diagonal matrix
with $`v`$ on its diagonal. For $`M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}`$,
$`i,j\in[n]`$, denote $`M[i,j]`$ the $`(i,j)`$th entry, $`M[i]`$ the
$`i`$th row, and $`M[:,j]`$ the $`j`$th column of $`M`$.
$`O^{k\times k}`$ is the set of $`(k\times k)`$ orthogonal matrices.
$`\mathbf{1}`$ is the all-$`1`$’s vector. $`\forall x\in V`$,
$`e_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$ is the unit vector along dimension indexed
by $`x\in V`$. For an undirected, unweighted graph $`G=(V,E)`$, for any
$`x,y\in V`$,   $`\textup{dist}(x,y)`$ is the minimum number of edges of
any path connecting $`x`$ and $`y`$ in $`G`$. $`\deg(x)`$ denotes the
degree of node $`x\in V`$. For $`x\in V,r\in\mathbb{N}`$, denote
$`B(x,r):=\{x^{\prime}\in V:\textup{dist}(x,x^{\prime})\leq r\}`$ and
$`\partial B(x,r):=B(x,r)-B(x,r-1),\,B(x,-1):=\emptyset`$. For set
$`S\subset V,`$ let $`B(S,r):=\bigcup_{v\in S}B(v,r)`$. For
$`\pi,f,f^{\prime}:V\to(0,\infty)`$, let
$`\langle f,f^{\prime}\rangle_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}:=\sum_{x\in V}f(x)f^{\prime}(x)\frac{1}{\pi(x)}`$
and
$`||f||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}:=\langle f,f\rangle_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$.
Let $`\Delta(V)`$ denote the set of probability distributions whose
support is contained in the set $`V`$. For $`D\in\Delta(V)`$,
$`\operatorname{supp}(D)`$ is its support. For $`g:V\to\Delta(V)`$,
$`g\#D\in\Delta(V)`$ is the distribution of $`y`$, drawn according to
this process: $`x\sim D,y\sim g(x)`$. We say an algorithm has
independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sample access to $`D`$
if it has an oracle which it can query for i.i.d. samples $`x\sim D`$.

##### Markov Chains on Graphs and Isoperimetric Inequality.

[Section A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
has more-detailed preliminaries. Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be an undirected,
connected graph with a countable set of vertices. Let $`(V,P)`$ denote
an irreducible, reversible Markov chain with transition matrix
$`P\in[0,1]^{|V|\times|V|}`$ and invariant measure
$`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$ where reversibility means that
$`\forall x,y\in V,\pi(x)P[x,y]=\pi(y)P[y,x]`$. Let $`E(P)`$ be the set
of unordered tuples $`(x,y)`$ where $`P[x,y]>0`$. Given $`e\in E(P)`$ we
will write $`e=(e^{-},e^{+})`$, but the choice of which end-point is
$`e^{-}`$ and which is $`e^{+}`$ does not matter for our analysis. If
$`E(P)\subset E`$, then $`(V,P)`$ is nearest-neighbor-type random walk
(Markov chain). The simple random walk $`P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$ is a
Markov chain where every node $`x`$ transitions uniformly to its
neighbors $`N(x)`$. For any $`A\subset V`$, let $`\partial A`$ be the
set of all edges in $`E(P)`$ with one endpoint in $`A`$ and the other in
$`V-A`$. Let $`\pi(A):=\sum_{x\in A}\pi(x)`$ and
$`a(\partial A):=\sum_{(e^{-},e^{+})\in\partial A}\pi(e^{-})P[e^{-},e^{+}]=\sum_{e^{-}\in A,e^{+}\notin A}\pi(e^{-})P[e^{-},e^{+}]`$.

###### Definition 3.1 (Isoperimetric Inequality).

A Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ satisfies Strong Isoperimetric Inequality, IS,
if there exists a constant $`\kappa>0`$ such that for every subset of
finite cardinality $`A\subset V`$,
$`\pi(A)\leq\kappa\cdot a(\partial A)`$.

##### Contrastive Learning.

[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
contains more detailed preliminaries. Contrastive learning defines an
algorithm for learning an embedding model that maps elements from a
domain $`V`$ (e.g. the set of real-world images) into Euclidean space
$`\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ for some $`k\in\mathbb{N}`$. It is most notably used
for training neural networks as embedding models [Hadsell et al.
(2006)](#bib.bib44); [van den Oord et al. (2019)](#bib.bib42); [Chen et
al. (2020)](#bib.bib43). We will use the setup of [HaoChen et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib6), which we describe below.

Let $`\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}`$ denote the class of all functions mapping
$`V`$ to $`\mathbb{R}^{k}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\subset\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}`$ denote the
hypothesis class of models $`h_{\theta}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ which we
assume contains the ground-truth embedding model of the learning task.
Contrastive learning defines two distributions of pairs of elements in
$`V`$: a positive pair distribution $`D_{+}\in\Delta(V\times V)`$ and a
negative pair distribution $`D_{-}\in\Delta(V\times V)`$. Given i.i.d.
samples from both distributions, the trained model is encouraged to
embed two elements sampled from a positive pair $`(x,y)\sim D_{+}`$
close together in Euclidean space, while embedding two elements sampled
from a negative pair $`(x,x^{\prime})\sim D_{-}`$ far apart in Euclidean
space. These two distributions of pairs of elements are used to define a
contrastive loss, and training the model amounts to minimizing an
empirical estimate of the contrastive loss from finite samples.

Let the domain $`V`$ consist of $`N\in\mathbb{N}`$ elements, where $`N`$
is large but finite. We will identify $`V`$ with $`[N]`$ here for
simplicity. Define $`\mu\in\Delta([N])`$ as the base distribution and
$`Q\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}`$ as an augmentation scheme. Overloading
notation, we can alternatively view $`Q:[N]\to\Delta(N)`$ as a mapping
from an element $`x`$ to a distribution $`Q(x)`$ over augmentations of
$`x`$. For every $`x\in[N]`$, $`Q(x)`$, equals the $`x`$-th row of the
matrix-representation of $`Q`$. For $`h_{\theta}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$,
define the population contrastive loss
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}:\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}\to\mathbb{R}`$ as

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}(h_{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{-})\sim D_{-}}(h_{\theta}(x)^{\top}h_{\theta}(x^{-}))^{2}-2\cdot\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{+})\sim D_{+}}h_{\theta}(x)^{\top}h_{\theta}(x^{+})`$ |     | (3.1) |

Positive pairs $`(x,x^{+})\sim D_{+}`$ are sampled by first sampling an
element from the base distribution, $`z\sim\mu`$ and then sampling the
pair elements as independent augmentations $`x\sim Q(z)`$,
$`x^{+}\sim Q(z)`$, returning $`(x,x^{+})`$. Negative pairs
$`(x,x^{-})\sim D_{-}`$ are sampled by first sampling $`z,z^{-}\sim\mu`$
independently and then sampling $`x\sim Q(z),x^{-}\sim Q(z^{-})`$,
returning $`(x,x^{-})`$.

For a dataset $`\{\overline{x}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\subset V`$, define the
empirical contrastive loss
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}:\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}\to\mathbb{R}`$
as:

|                   |                                                                                                                                                                                 |                                                                                       |                       |       |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ----- |
|                   |                                                                                                                                                                                 | $`\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}(h_{\theta^{\prime}}):=`$           |                       | (3.2) |
|                   |                                                                                                                                                                                 | $`\displaystyle-\frac{2}{n}\sum*{i\in[n]}\mathbb{E}*{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim Q(\cdot | \overline{x}\_{i}),\\ |
| x^{+}\sim Q(\cdot | \overline{x}_{i})\end{subarray}}(h_{\theta^{\prime}}(x)^{\top}h*{\theta^{\prime}}(x^{+}))+\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum*{i,j\in[n],i\neq j}\mathbb{E}\_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim Q(\cdot | \overline{x}\_{i}),\\                                                                 |
| x^{-}\sim Q(\cdot | \overline{x}_{j})\end{subarray}}(h_{\theta^{\prime}}(x)^{\top}h\_{\theta^{\prime}}(x^{-}))^{2}`$                                                                                |                                                                                       | (3.3)                 |

Claim D.2 of [HaoChen et al. (2022)](#bib.bib6) shows that
$`\mathbb{E}_{\{\overline{x}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\sim\mu}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}(h_{\theta})=\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}(h_{\theta})`$,
i.e. that $`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$ is unbiased. Define
the empirical risk minimizer (ERM) as follows.

###### Definition 3.2 (ERM, $`\epsilon`$-minimizer).

The empirical risk minimizer (ERM) is any embedding function of
$`h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ that minimizes
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$ over
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$.

|     |                                                                                                                                                           |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle h_{\theta}\leftarrow\arg\min_{h_{\theta^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}(h_{\theta^{\prime}})`$ |     | (3.4) |

For $`\epsilon>0`$, an $`\epsilon`$-minimizer of
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$ is any embedding function of
$`h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ where:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                              |     |       |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}(h_{\theta})\leq\min_{h_{\theta^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}(h_{\theta^{\prime}})+\epsilon`$ |     | (3.5) |

We will also call an $`\epsilon`$-minimizer of
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$ an $`\epsilon`$-ERM.

[Algorithm 7](#alg7 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is an algorithm that learns an embedding model using empirical risk
minimization, given i.i.d. sample access to base distribution
$`D\in\Delta(V)`$ and augmentation function $`Q:V\to\Delta(V)`$. To
quantify the statistical generalization properties of the ERM, we
introduce the following notion of Rademacher complexity.

###### Definition 3.3 (Rademacher Complexity).

The Rademacher complexity of function class $`\mathcal{F}`$ of models
$`\mathcal{F}\ni h:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ on $`n`$ datapoints is:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                       |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F}):=\max_{x_{1},\ldots x_{n}\in V}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F},i\in[k]}\frac{1}{n}(\sum_{j\in[n]}\sigma_{j}h_{i}(x_{j}))`$ |     | (3.6) |

## 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline

### 4.1 Primitive Assumptions

With $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ denoting the iteration index, the primary goal
of the training algorithm is to produce a prover $`f`$ which can prove
as many theorems as possible. One way a training algorithm can achieve
this is by producing a sequence of provers
$`\{f_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ where the prover $`f_{t+1}`$ can prove
more theorems than prover $`f_{t}`$ for every $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$. The
following assumptions define a set of core primitives for designing such
a training algorithm.

[Assumption 1](#Thmassumption1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
assumes i.i.d. sample access to an initial training distribution
$`D_{0}`$ of theorems where for every theorem $`x`$ in the support of
$`D_{0}`$, the proof of $`x`$ is known. This means that we have
efficient access to a proof of $`x`$, either because it is recorded
explicitly in some database of (theorem, proof) pairs, or because we
have access to a prover $`f`$ where
$`\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq\Omega(1)`$. The latter condition means
that given $`x`$ and $`f`$, the proof of $`x`$ can be efficiently
sampled in $`O(1)`$ calls to $`f`$, with high probability.

###### Assumption 1.

(Cold-Start Dataset) We are given access to an oracle that provides
i.i.d. samples from $`D_{0}\in\Delta(V)`$ where the proof of every
theorem $`x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_{0})`$ is known.

An example of $`D_{0}`$ would be a distribution of
elementary-school-level math problems.

[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
describes the ability of a model, trained on a distribution $`D`$ of
theorems via i.i.d. samples, to generalize in-domain to $`D`$. We
justify it with statistical learning theory in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Assumption 2.

(Training) Let $`p\in(0,1),p=\Theta(1)`$ be a universal constant. Let
$`D\in\Delta(V)`$ be a distribution of theorems where
$`\forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D)`$, the proof of $`x`$ is known.
Then, $`\forall\,\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)`$, with
$`n=\Theta(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})\log\frac{1}{\delta}}{\epsilon^{2}(1-p)^{2}})`$
where $`\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})`$ is an
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$-dependent constant, we can train a
prover $`f`$ using $`n`$ i.i.d. samples from $`D`$ such that with
probability at least $`1-\delta`$, we have that $`f`$ satisfies:

|     |                                                                                      |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$ |     | (4.1) |

The requirement of
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
that the proof of every theorem in $`\operatorname{supp}(D)`$ is known
can also be thought of as requiring a training distribution of (theorem,
proof) pairs, where every theorem in the support of the training
distribution must have a correct proof associated with it. This
requirement is necessary, as otherwise it would be possible to train a
model to have high success rate on arbitrarily hard theorems for which
we do not know the proof.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be the theorem graph.
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
says that the edge set $`E`$ is where the success rate of any prover in
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ is not too different between two
theorems connected by an edge.

###### Assumption 3.

(Continuity of Success Rate) With $`p\in(0,1)`$ defined as in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
assume for all $`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, for all
$`(x,y)\in E`$, that
$`|\operatorname{succ}(x,f)-\operatorname{succ}(y,f)|\leq\frac{p}{2}`$

In
[Assumption 4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
we assume access to a neighbor oracle $`N`$ as a primitive.

###### Assumption 4.

(Neighbor Access) For any $`x\in V,`$ let
$`N(x):=\{y\in V:(x,y)\in E\}`$. We assume oracle access to a neighbor
oracle $`N:V\to 2^{V}`$, which on input of any $`x\in V`$, returns
$`N(x)`$.

Assumptions
[2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
–
[4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
enable a training algorithm to run the following at each iteration.
First, expand the current set of known theorems by one step via the
neighbor oracle $`N`$
([Assumption 4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
Second,
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
ensures that unseen theorems have success rate at least $`p/2`$ under
the current prover, enabling the proofs of the unseen theorems to be
efficiently sampled. In general, note that if we have access to a prover
$`f`$ whose success rate on theorem $`x`$ is reasonably high
($`\geq p/2`$, where $`p\geq\Omega(1)`$ by
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
then the proof of $`x`$ can be efficiently sampled and become known.
Finally, a new prover is trained on the expanded set of theorems via
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is necessary to our analysis because standard statistical learning
theory arguments rely on exchangeability between training and test
distributions and therefore do not by themselves justify this
out-of-distribution step.

We do not require the edge set $`E`$ to have an interpretable
definition. We only require $`E`$ to satisfy
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and
[Assumption 4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
One example instantiation of the theorem graph is where $`V`$ is the set
of theorems corresponding to discrete logarithm instances in a fixed
cyclic group. Fix a cyclic group $`\mathbb{G}`$ of prime order $`q`$
with generator $`g\in\mathbb{G}`$. For each $`a\in\mathbb{Z}_{q}`$, let
$`h_{a}=g^{a}`$, and let $`x_{a}\in V`$ denote the theorem:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                           |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | “Given cyclic group $`\mathbb{G}`$ of prime order $`q`$, and given $`g,g^{-1},h_{a}\in\mathbb{G},\text{ there exists }z\in\mathbb{Z}_{q}\text{ such that }g^{z}=h_{a}`$.” |     |

The proof of $`x_{a}`$ is the unique exponent $`f_{*}(x_{a})=a`$. Define
the edge set $`E`$ by
$`(x_{a},x_{b})\in E\iff b-a\in\{-1,+1\}\pmod{q}.`$ Thus, the theorem
graph is a cycle over the discrete logarithm instances. This edge set
satisfies
[Assumption 4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
since given the theorem $`x_{a}=(\mathbb{G},g,g^{-1},h_{a})`$, the
neighbor oracle can compute $`N(x_{a})=\{x_{a+1},x_{a-1}\}`$, where
$`x_{a+1}`$ has target $`h_{a}g=g^{a+1}`$, and $`x_{a-1}`$ has target
$`h_{a}g^{-1}=g^{a-1}`$. Finally,
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
amounts to the property that adjacent discrete-log instances have
similar success rates for the prover class:
$`(x_{a},x_{a+1})\in E\implies\forall f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}},|\operatorname{succ}(x_{a},f)-\operatorname{succ}(x_{a+1},f)|\leq\frac{p}{2}.`$
This property is conceivable for some prover classes since $`x_{a}`$ and
$`x_{a+1}`$ are not substantially different: given $`g`$ and its inverse
$`g^{-1}`$, an instance with target $`h_{a+1}`$ can be reduced to the
adjacent instance with target $`h_{a}`$ by multiplying by $`g^{-1}`$,
i.e. $`h_{a+1}g^{-1}=g^{a+1}g^{-1}=g^{a}=h_{a}.`$ Thus, any prover that
can prove $`h_{a}`$ can prove $`h_{a+1}`$ by first reducing $`h_{a+1}`$
to $`h_{a}`$, running the original prover, and then adding $`1`$ to the
resulting exponent. For model classes $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$
that can exploit such reductions, it is conceivable that neighboring
instances $`x_{a}`$ and $`x_{a\pm 1}`$ have similar success rates.

### 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm

##### Conjecturer.

In STP [Dong and Ma (2025)](#bib.bib10), the conjecturer is a mapping
that takes as input a theorem $`x`$, its proof $`f_{*}(x)`$, a lemma
$`l`$ used in $`f_{*}(x)`$, and a system prompt; it returns a theorem
$`c`$ related to $`x`$. We study a simplification where the conjecturer
maps a theorem to a distribution of theorems.

###### Definition 4.1.

(Conjecturer) For graph $`G=(V,E)`$, a conjecturer is a mapping
$`C:V\to\Delta(V)`$. Given i.i.d. sample access to input distribution
$`D\in\Delta(V)`$, the conjecturer returns i.i.d. sample access to
$`D^{\prime}=C\#D\in\Delta(V)`$.

A reversible conjecturer is a special type of conjecturer, specified by
a set of symmetric, non-negative edge weights $`w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{+}`$,
where $`\forall x,y\in V,w(x,y)=w(y,x)\geq 0`$. Denote
$`P_{w}\in[0,1]^{|V|\times|V|}`$ as the matrix representation of $`w`$,
defined as:
$`\forall x,y\in V,P_{w}[x,y]=\frac{w(x,y)}{\sum_{z\in N(x)}w(x,z)}`$.
Denote $`C_{w}:V\to\Delta(V)`$ as the sampler representation of $`w`$,
defined as: $`\forall x\in V,C_{w}(x)=P_{w}[x]`$. Note that the
transition matrix $`P_{w}`$ defines a nearest-neighbor-type reversible
random walk over state-set $`V`$, with stationary measure
$`\pi_{w}:V\to(0,\infty)`$, where
$`\forall x\in V,\pi_{w}(x)\propto\sum_{z\in N(x)}w(x,z)=:w(x)`$.

These three representations $`C_{w},P_{w},w`$ are equivalent and
uniquely determined given any of the other. Sometimes we will write the
tuple $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$, where $`C_{w}`$ and $`P_{w}`$ are defined in
terms of $`w`$ as above. When the context requires just $`C_{w}`$, we
will identify $`C_{w}`$ with the conjecturer.

For instance, when $`\forall x\in V,z\in N(x),w(x,z)=1`$ and for
$`z\notin N(x),w(x,z)=0`$, then $`C_{w}(x)=\textup{Unif}(N(x))`$, so
that $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ defines a simple random walk over $`G`$, with
$`\pi_{w}(x)\propto\deg(x)`$.

##### Prover-Conjecturer System.

This section provides sufficient conditions for a prover-conjecturer
system
([Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
to learn to prove more theorems across iterations.
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
assumes the conjecturer $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$, defining Markov chain
$`(V,P_{w})`$, satisfies a connectivity assumption.

###### Assumption 5.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a connected graph where the number of vertices is
countably infinite ($`|V|=\infty`$) and each vertex has finite degree.
Assume that the Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ for $`G`$ satisfies the strong
isoperimetric inequality, IS, defined in
[Definition 3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 3.1 (Isoperimetric Inequality). ‣ Markov Chains on Graphs and Isoperimetric Inequality. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

At iteration $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, the prover-conjecturer system
([Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
initialized with conjecturer $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$, has i.i.d. sample
access to $`D_{t}\in\Delta(V)`$, a training distribution over theorems
whose proofs are known. It trains prover
$`f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ on $`D_{t}`$ via
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Finally, it constructs i.i.d. sample access to a new distribution over
theorems, $`D_{t+1}\in\Delta(V)`$ using
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Given $`D_{t}`$,
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
applies the conjecturer $`C_{w}`$ to $`D_{t}`$, yielding
$`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$. Theorems with low pass rate under $`f_{t}`$ are
filtered out, yielding $`D_{t+1}`$.

[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
uses
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
as a subroutine to construct $`D_{t+1}`$ from $`D_{t}`$.
[Algorithm 3](#alg3 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is a practical approximation to
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and it can be substituted in for
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
In
[Algorithm 3](#alg3 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
for a sufficiently large rollout-budget
$`m\geq\Theta(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\log\frac{1}{\delta_{\textup{samp}}})`$, by
standard concentration inequalities [Hoeffding (1963)](#bib.bib41); [Ma
(2022)](#bib.bib3), we have that $`\forall x\in V`$, with probability at
least $`1-\delta_{\textup{samp}}`$,
$`|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbf{1}[\textup{Ver}(x,\pi_{i})=1]-\operatorname{succ}(x,f)|<p/2`$.
Thus, with high probability, if $`\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p/2`$,
then
$`\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbf{1}[\textup{Ver}(x,\pi_{i})=1]>0`$, so
that at least one empirically-sampled proof $`\pi`$ of theorem $`x`$ is
correct.

1: Prover class $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, reversible
conjecturer $`C_{w}:V\to\Delta(V)`$ as in
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
parameters $`\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)`$, threshold $`p>0`$

2: Acquire theorem distribution $`D_{0}\in\Delta(V)`$ using
[Assumption 1](#Thmassumption1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

3: for $`t=0,1,2,\ldots`$ do

4:   Given i.i.d. sample access to $`D_{t}`$, train prover
$`f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ on $`D_{t}`$ to accuracy
$`\epsilon`$ and failure probability $`\delta`$ using
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

5:   Define i.i.d. sample access to $`D_{t+1}`$ by applying
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with input $`(D_{t},f_{t},C_{w},p/2)`$

Algorithm 1 Prover-Conjecturer System

1: i.i.d. sample access to $`D\in\Delta(V)`$, prover
$`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, conjecturer
$`C_{w}:V\to\Delta(V)`$, threshold $`q>0`$, verifier
$`\textup{Ver}:V\times\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}`$, and oracle access to
$`\operatorname{succ}(\cdot,f)`$

2: i.i.d. sample access to $`D^{\prime}\in\Delta(V)`$

3: i.i.d. sampler for $`D^{\prime}`$:

4:   repeat

5:    Draw theorem $`x\sim D`$

6:    Sample $`x^{\prime}\sim C_{w}(x)`$

7:   until $`\operatorname{succ}(x^{\prime},f)\geq q`$

8:   Sample and record a correct proof of $`x^{\prime}`$ from $`f`$,
checking correctness using Ver.

9:   return $`x^{\prime}`$

Algorithm 2 Pass-Rate-Oracle-Based Sampler

1: i.i.d. sample access to $`D\in\Delta(V)`$, prover
$`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, conjecturer kernel $`C_{w}`$,
rollout budget $`m\in\mathbb{N}`$, and verifier
$`\textup{Ver}:V\times\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}`$.

2: i.i.d. sample access to distribution $`D^{\prime}\in\Delta(V)`$

3: i.i.d. sampler for $`D^{\prime}`$:

4:   repeat

5:    Draw theorem $`x\sim D`$

6:    Sample $`x^{\prime}\sim C_{w}(x)`$

7:    Sample candidate proofs of $`x^{\prime}`$ from $`f`$ as:
$`\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m}\sim f(x^{\prime})`$

8:    if there exists $`j\in[m]`$ such that
$`\textup{Ver}(x^{\prime},\pi_{j})=1`$ then

9:      Record proof $`\pi_{j}`$ of theorem $`x^{\prime}`$.

10:      return $`x^{\prime}`$    

11:   until a theorem $`x^{\prime}`$ is returned

Algorithm 3 Empirical-Pass-Rate-Based Sampler

Due to the push-forward construction of $`D_{t+1}`$ from $`D_{t}`$ in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
for every $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, sampling from $`D_{t}`$ requires first
sampling $`x_{0}\sim D_{0}`$, then applying $`t`$ push-forward
transformations to yield $`x_{i}\sim D_{j}`$, for all $`j\in[t]`$. In
particular, first draw a large number $`N_{0}`$ of i.i.d. samples
$`x_{0}^{(i)}\sim D_{0}`$, $`i\in[N_{0}]`$. At every iteration
$`j\in\{0\}\cup[t]`$, suppose inductively that there are $`N_{j}`$
remaining unused i.i.d. samples from $`D_{j}`$. Use
$`\Theta(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})\log\frac{1}{\delta}}{\epsilon^{2}(1-p)^{2}})`$
of the $`N_{j}`$ samples to train prover $`f_{j}`$ via
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Of the unused samples, apply the conjecturer to map $`x_{j}^{(i)}`$ to
$`y_{j}^{(i)}\sim C_{w}(x_{j}^{(i)})`$. Discard $`y_{j}^{(i)}`$ if
$`\operatorname{succ}(y_{j}^{(i)},f_{j})<p/2`$, else let
$`x_{j+1}^{(i)}:=y_{j}^{(i)}`$. Let $`N_{j+1}`$ denote the number of
remaining samples. Note that if prover $`f_{j}`$ is successfully trained
according to
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
to where
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{j}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{j})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
then by
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{j},x^{\prime}\sim C_{w}(x)}[\operatorname{succ}(x^{\prime},f_{j})\geq p/2]\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
so that by standard concentration inequalities,
$`N_{j+1}\gtrapprox(1-\epsilon)N_{j}`$. In the worst case, we have that
$`\forall j\in[t],N_{j}\approx N_{0}(1-\epsilon)^{j}`$, so that the
number of oracle calls to $`D_{0}`$ required to sample from $`D_{j}`$
grows as $`(\frac{1}{1-\epsilon})^{j}`$.

### 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for [Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that on an infinite graph, with a reversible conjecturer
([Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
that induces a random walk that satisfies the Strong Isoperimetric
Inequality
([Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
and for training error threshold $`\epsilon<\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$,
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
generates a sequence of provers $`\{f_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ such that
$`\forall t\in\mathbb{N},`$ the size of the $`t`$-th prover’s knowledge
set $`|\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p\}|`$ is exponential
in $`t`$.

###### Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of [Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a theorem graph with $`|V|=\infty`$ and
$`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ be a reversible conjecturer as in
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Suppose $`(V,P_{w})`$ satisfies Assumption
[5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with Isoperimetric constant $`\kappa>0`$. Let $`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$ be
an invariant measure of $`(V,P_{w})`$. Suppose Assumptions
[1](#Thmassumption1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")-[4](#Thmassumption4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
hold, with universal constant $`p\in(0,1)`$ as in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and that $`\pi`$ is chosen so that $`\sup_{z\in V}\pi(z)<\infty`$ and
$`0<||D_{0}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}<\infty`$. For any
$`\delta,\epsilon\in(0,1)`$,
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
produces a sequence of provers $`\{f_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ where
$`\forall t\in\mathbb{N}`$, with probability at least
$`1-(t+1)\,\delta`$,

|     |                 |                                                |                                                         |
| --- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle | \{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f\_{t})\geq p\} | \geq\frac{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}{(\sup\_{z\in V}\pi(z))\cdot |     | D\_{0} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}}\cdot(\frac{1-\epsilon}{1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}})^{2t}`$ |     | (4.2) |

To prove
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
we show that for every $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$,
$`||D_{t+1}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}\leq(\frac{||P_{w}^{\top}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}{1-\epsilon})^{2}\cdot`$
$`||D_{t}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$, where
$`||P_{w}^{\top}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ is the operator
norm of $`P_{w}^{\top}`$ in the Hilbert space $`\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$. By
[Corollary A.15](#A1.Thmtheorem15 "Corollary A.15. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
since $`(V,P_{w})`$ satisfies
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
then
$`||P_{w}^{\top}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$.
Finally,
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
follows from
[Lemma E.1](#A5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma E.1. ‣ Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
which lower bounds $`|\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p\}|`$
using $`\frac{1}{||D_{t}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}`$. The full proof is
in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

Thus, if the simple random walk $`P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$ over the theorem
graph satisfies IS (i.e. for any finite
$`A\subset V,\frac{|\{(e^{-},e^{+})\in E\;:\;e^{-}\in A,\;e^{+}\notin A\}|}{\sum_{x\in A}\deg(x)}\geq\frac{1}{\kappa}`$),
then
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with a conjecturer, whose transition matrix is $`P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$,
generates a sequence of provers $`\{f_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ whose
knowledge set grows exponentially.

## 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm

### 5.1 Diversity Measure

Unlike
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
suppose for simplicity the theorem graph has a finite but large number
of nodes and $`||\pi||_{1}=1`$. ²² 2 We believe the following analysis
can be extended to infinite graphs. The following ideas can be
instantiated with any $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, but practically $`\tau`$
should be a small non-zero natural number. The main object of interest
in this section is the $`\tau`$-expanded knowledge set of a prover
$`f`$.

###### Definition 5.1.

With universal $`p\in(0,1)`$ in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
for any $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, $`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$,
let
$`K^{p}_{\tau}(f):=B(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\},\tau)`$
$`=\{x^{\prime}\in V:\exists x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\textup{ and }\textup{dist}(x,x^{\prime})\leq\tau\}`$.
We call $`K^{p}(f):=K_{0}^{p}(f)`$ the knowledge set of $`f`$ and
$`K^{p}_{\tau}(f)`$ the $`\tau`$-expanded knowledge set.

We define an operational notion of diversity of $`f`$’s knowledge as the
size of $`K^{p}_{\tau}(f)`$. $`K^{p}_{\tau}(f)`$ can be interpreted as
the set of theorems that $`f`$ can prove by performing $`\tau`$ steps of
“reasoning" at inference time to reduce the input theorem into one it
knows how to prove.
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In A Baseline Conjecturing Algorithm. ‣ 1.1 Technical Overview ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
depicts two provers $`f_{1}`$, $`f_{2}`$ whose knowledge sets are the
same size $`|K^{p}(f_{1})|=|K^{p}(f_{2})|`$, but where their
$`\tau`$-step expansions are of different sizes:
$`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f_{1})|\ll|K^{p}_{\tau}(f_{2})|`$. Thus, $`f_{2}`$’s
knowledge is more diverse than $`f_{1}`$’s. Identifying diversity with
$`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f)|`$ reflects the intuition that knowing a diverse set
of proof ideas is useful to a prover $`f`$ as it increases the set of
theorems that $`f`$ can prove by combining known proof ideas.

Let $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ be a baseline conjecturer satisfying
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and for convenience denote $`P:=P_{w}`$. Our goal is to design an
improved conjecturer that generates a sequence of training distributions
$`\{D_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ where at each $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ prover
$`f_{t}`$ is trained on $`D_{t}`$, and where $`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f_{t})|`$
increases quickly with $`t`$. In fact,
[Lemma 5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 5.3 (Large "Div"^𝑃*𝜏 implies large 𝐾^𝑝*𝜏). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
(proved in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
shows that for each $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ it is reasonable to maximize
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t})`$
([Definition 5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
a diversity measure of the training distribution $`D_{t}`$.

###### Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure).

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a theorem graph with $`P`$ being the transition
matrix of any reversible, nearest-neighbor-type random walk with
stationary measure $`\pi`$. For any parameter $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, and
any $`\mu\in\Delta(V)`$, define:

|     |                                                         |     |                    |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------------------ | --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textup{Div}^{P}\_{\tau}(\mu):=\frac{1}{ |     | \mu^{\top}P^{\tau} |     | ^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{x\in V}(\mu^{\top}P^{\tau}e\_{x})^{2}\frac{1}{\pi(x)}}`$ |     | (5.1) |

###### Lemma 5.3 (Large $`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}`$ implies large $`K^{p}_{\tau}`$).

Let $`p\in[0,1]`$ be a universal constant in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Instantiate $`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}:\Delta(V)\to\mathbb{R}`$ with the
transition matrix $`P`$ of any reversible, nearest-neighbor-type random
walk. For any $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, any prover
$`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, and any theorem distribution
$`D\in\Delta(V)`$, the $`\tau`$-expanded knowledge set of $`f`$
satisfies:

|     |                 |                  |                                                                                                                         |
| --- | --------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle | K^{p}\_{\tau}(f) | \geq\frac{(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p])^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\textup{Div}^{P}\_{\tau}(D)`$ |     | (5.2) |

If prover $`f`$ is successfully trained on theorem distribution $`D`$
via
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
then
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$.
By
[Lemma 5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 5.3 (Large "Div"^𝑃*𝜏 implies large 𝐾^𝑝*𝜏). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
$`|K_{\tau}^{p}(f)|\geq\frac{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D)`$,
so maximizing $`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D)`$ of the training
distribution is a reasonable proxy for maximizing $`|K_{\tau}^{p}(f)|`$.

We note that in the setting of
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
where
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
holds for random walk $`(V,P)`$, then maximizing $`|B(K^{p}(f),\tau)|`$
reduces to maximizing $`|K^{p}(f)|`$. When $`P=P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$,
then
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
implies for bounded-degree graphs that there is a reasonable constant
$`c`$ where for any finite
$`A\subset V,|B(A,\tau)|\geq\exp(c\,\tau)|A|`$. That is, any finite
subset of theorems is diverse. More generally, if
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
holds for $`P`$ (not necessarily $`P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$), then for
$`\{D_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$ generated as
$`D_{t+1}^{\top}=D_{t}^{\top}P`$, we have
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t})=\frac{1}{||D_{t+\tau}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}`$,
where $`\pi^{\top}P=\pi^{\top}`$. Because the proof of
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
implies fast exponential decay of $`||D_{t}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ as
a function of $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ for every $`t`$, it follows that
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t})`$ grows exponentially for each $`t`$.
In short, when
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
holds, then the two objectives $`|K^{p}(f)|`$ and $`|K^{p}_{\tau}(f)|`$
are aligned. As such, the more interesting setting for studying
diversity is when
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
does not hold for the baseline random walk $`P`$. When
$`P=P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$, some intuitive graphs where
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
does not hold are graphs consisting of multiple poorly-interconnected
clusters, such as that depicted in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In A Baseline Conjecturing Algorithm. ‣ 1.1 Technical Overview ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
or
[Figure 2](#A6.F2 "In Appendix F Figures ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
For a graph like in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In A Baseline Conjecturing Algorithm. ‣ 1.1 Technical Overview ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
the choice of which nodes to include in $`K^{p}(f)`$ will greatly impact
$`K^{p}_{\tau}(f)`$, making the problem of maximizing both $`K^{p}(f)`$
and $`K^{p}_{\tau}(f)`$ non-trivial.

### 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm

[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is a conjecturer that generates a sequence of training distributions
$`\{D_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}`$, with the aim to maximize
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t})`$ at each $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, for a
chosen hyper-parameter $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$. This maximization cannot
easily be done in closed form, as the conjecturer is restricted to
generate $`D_{t+1}`$ from $`D_{t}`$ by one step of a
nearest-neighbor-type random walk. Instead, fixing
$`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$,
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
defines a push-forward map $`C:V\to\Delta(V)`$ where for any $`x\in V`$,
$`C(x)\in\Delta(N(x))`$ is supported on neighbors $`N(x)`$ of $`x`$. The
weighting of $`C(x)`$ is determined by maximizing
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(C(x))`$.

|     |                                        |                                                                                                                                                                              |     |       |
| --- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\forall x\in V,\,C(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\max_{\mu\in\Delta(N(x))}\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(\mu)=\arg\min_{\mu\in\Delta(N(x))}\mu^{\top}P^{\tau}\textup{diag}(1/\pi)(P^{\tau})^{\top}\mu`$ |     | (5.3) |

Where $`\forall z\in V,\textup{diag}(1/\pi)[z,z]=\frac{1}{\pi(z)}`$.
This optimization problem can be solved given the matrix,
$`M(x,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^{|N(x)|\times|N(x)|}`$ where for any
$`y,y^{\prime}\in N(x)`$, the $`(y,y^{\prime})`$-th entry is:
$`M(x,\tau)[y,y^{\prime}]:=e_{y}^{\top}P^{\tau}\textup{diag}(1/\pi)(P^{\tau})^{\top}e_{y^{\prime}}`$.
We can characterize $`M(x,\tau)`$ in terms of diffusion embeddings of
the neighbors of $`x`$, where a diffusion embedding embeds any node
$`z\in V`$ to a vector $`p^{\tau}(z)`$ representing the probability
distribution of a $`\tau`$-step random walk started at $`z`$ according
to transition matrix $`P`$.

###### Definition 5.4.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a connected, undirected graph, with $`P`$ being the
transition matrix of a reversible random walk over $`V`$, with
stationary measure $`\pi`$. For all
$`\tau\in\mathbb{N},\forall x\in V`$, define $`p^{\tau}(x)`$ as the
scale-$`\tau`$ diffusion embedding of $`x`$ where:

|     |                                                 |                                                               |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle p^{\tau}(x)`$                   | $`\displaystyle:=(P^{\tau})^{\top}e\_{x}\in[0,1]^{            | V   | }`$   |     | (5.4) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\forall z\in V,\,p^{\tau}(x,z)`$ | $`\displaystyle:=e_{z}^{\top}(P^{\tau})^{\top}e_{x}\in[0,1]`$ |     | (5.5) |

For every $`x,y\in V`$, define the scale-$`\tau`$ diffusion similarity
as

|     |                                                                                                                                                                          |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(x,y):=\langle p^{\tau}(x),p^{\tau}(y)\rangle_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}:=\sum_{z\in V}p^{\tau}(x,z)\,p^{\tau}(y,z)\,\frac{1}{\pi(z)}`$ |     | (5.6) |

and the scale-$`\tau`$ diffusion distance [Coifman and Lafon
(2006)](#bib.bib36); [Yao (2011)](#bib.bib8) as

|     |                                                    |     |                         |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----------------------- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\rho^{\textup{diff}}\_{\tau}(x,y):= |     | p^{\tau}(x)-p^{\tau}(y) |     | _{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}:=\sqrt{\sum_{z\in V}(p^{\tau}(x,z)-p^{\tau}(y,z))^{2}\frac{1}{\pi(z)}}`$ |     | (5.7) |

For any $`y,y^{\prime}\in N(x)`$, the $`(y,y^{\prime})`$-th entry of
$`M(x,\tau)`$ is $`\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,y^{\prime})`$. Note
that the diffusion similarity requires computing $`\frac{1}{\pi(z)}`$
for relevant $`z\in V`$, but the stationary measure $`\pi(z)`$ need only
be computed up to a normalizing constant for the optimization problem in
[Equation 5.3](#S5.E3 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
For a conjecturer $`(C,P,w)`$ satisfying
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
$`\forall z\in V,\pi(z)\propto w(z)`$. Let
$`M^{\prime}(x,\tau)=P^{\tau}\textup{diag}(1/w)(P^{\tau})^{\top}`$ and
$`\forall z\in V`$, $`\textup{diag}(1/w)[z,z]=\frac{1}{w(z)}`$. With
regularization strength $`\eta\in[0,0.5]`$, $`\forall x\in V`$,
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
computes:

|     |                        |                                                                             |     |     |
| --- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle C(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\max\_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\Delta(N(x))\\ |

\mu(y)\geq\eta/\deg(x),\;\forall y\in N(x)\end{subarray}}\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(\mu)=\arg\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\Delta(N(x))\\
\mu(y)\geq\eta/\deg(x),\;\forall y\in N(x)\end{subarray}}\mu^{\top}M^{\prime}(x,\tau)\mu`$ | | (5.8) |

This mapping $`C:V\to\Delta(V)`$ defined in
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
can be substituted in for $`C_{w}`$ in line 4 of
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
called in line 4 of the prover-conjecturer system
([Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
If $`G`$ is finite, connected, undirected, and non-bipartite, the
regularization with $`\eta>0`$ ensures (via
[Lemma E.2](#A5.Thmtheorem2 "Lemma E.2. ‣ Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
the random walk induced by $`C`$ converges to a stationary measure,
eventually exploring the entire graph. Note that
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
uses
[Algorithm 5](#alg5 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
to compute diffusion embeddings.

1: $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, $`\eta\in[0,0.5]`$, reversible conjecturer
$`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ satisfying
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and i.i.d. sample access to $`D\in\Delta(V)`$

2: i.i.d. sample access to $`D^{\prime}=C\#D\in\Delta(V)`$

3: procedure $`C`$($`x`$)

4:   Compute $`p^{\tau}(u)`$ for all $`u\in N(x)`$ using
[Algorithm 5](#alg5 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$

5:   Let $`M^{\prime}(x,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^{|N(x)|\times|N(x)|}`$, with
$`(y,y^{\prime})`$-entry
$`\sum_{z}p^{\tau}(y,z)p^{\tau}(y^{\prime},z)\frac{1}{w(z)}`$,
$`\forall y,y^{\prime}\in N(x)`$

6:
  $`\displaystyle\mu_{x}\leftarrow\arg\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\Delta([|N(x)|])\\
\mu(i)\geq\eta/\deg(x)\;\forall i\in[|N(x)|]\end{subarray}}\mu^{\top}M^{\prime}(x,\tau)\mu`$

7:   Sample $`i\sim\mu_{x}`$ and return the $`i`$th neighbor of $`x`$

8: i.i.d. sampler for $`D^{\prime}=C\#D`$:

9:   Draw $`x\sim D`$, $`x^{\prime}\sim C(x)`$, and return
$`x^{\prime}`$

Algorithm 4 Improved Conjecturer

1: $`x\in V`$, $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, neighbor oracle $`N:V\to 2^{V}`$,
and reversible conjecturer $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$

2: $`p^{\tau}(x)`$

3: $`B_{-1}\leftarrow\emptyset`$, $`B_{0}\leftarrow\{x\}`$

4: for $`s=1,\ldots,\tau`$ do

5:   $`\partial B_{s-1}\leftarrow B_{s-1}\setminus B_{s-2}`$

6:   $`B_{s}\leftarrow B_{s-1}\cup\bigcup_{v\in\partial B_{s-1}}N(v)`$

7: $`S\leftarrow B_{\tau}`$; initialize
