Algorithm 5 Dynamic Program for $`p^{\tau}(x)`$

As a concrete guarantee,
[Proposition 5.6](#S5.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition 5.6. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
provably explores the theorem graph $`G`$ faster than a simple random
walk when $`G`$ is in a special class of clustered graphs.

###### Definition 5.5.

(Clique-Graph) Let parameters $`M`$ be the clique size, $`r`$ be the
meta-graph degree, and $`K`$ be the number of cliques. Let
$`Q=([K],E(Q))`$ be a finite connected, undirected, $`r`$-regular graph.
For $`i\in[K]`$, denote $`N_{Q}(i)\subset[K]`$ as the neighbors of $`i`$
in $`Q`$. Suppose there exists $`c\in[r]`$ where for every $`i\in[K]`$
and every two distinct neighbors $`j,k\in N_{Q}(i)`$,
$`|N_{Q}(j)\cap N_{Q}(k)|=c`$. For clique size $`M\geq 2`$, define the
graph $`G=G(Q,M)`$ by $`V=[K]\times[M]`$, where each
$`C_{i}:=\{i\}\times[M]`$ is a clique of size $`M`$. For every meta-edge
$`ij\in E(Q)`$ and $`a\in[M]`$, add the inter-clique edge
$`(i,a)\sim(j,a).`$

In the regime where the clique size $`M`$ is much larger than the
inter-cluster connectivity ($`M\gg r^{2}`$),
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
improves over the baseline simple-random-walk-based conjecturing
algorithm in that: both conjecturers define a random walk over the
meta-graph, but that of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
has a larger spectral gap [Levin et al. (2017)](#bib.bib4). The source
of the improvement is that
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
up-weights the probability of making inter-cluster transitions, compared
to the simple random walk. This becomes useful when the cluster size
$`M`$ is large, in which case the simple random walk can become stuck in
a cluster for a large number of steps.

###### Proposition 5.6.

(End-to-End Guarantee of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
Let $`Q=([K],E(Q))`$ be a finite connected, undirected, $`r`$-regular
graph. Let $`G=G(Q,M)`$ be a Clique-Graph satisfying
[Definition 5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Definition 5.5. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with meta-graph $`Q`$. Suppose $`M\geq r+3`$. Let $`P_{Q}`$ denote the
simple random walk over $`Q`$.
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
with parameters $`\tau=1,\eta=0`$, defines a random walk over the
meta-graph $`Q`$ with transition matrix
$`P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}=(\frac{1}{r+1}+O(\frac{1}{M}))I+(\frac{r}{r+1}+O(\frac{1}{M}))P_{Q}`$.
The simple random walk over $`G`$ defines a random walk over the
meta-graph $`Q`$ with transition matrix
$`P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}=\frac{M-1}{M-1+r}I+\frac{r}{M-1+r}P_{Q}`$.
Define the spectral gap of transition matrix $`P`$ as
$`\gamma(P):=1-\max(\lambda_{2}(P),|\lambda_{K}(P)|)`$. Then, there
exists a universal constant $`c>0`$ such that

|     |                                                                                                                  |     |       |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})\geq c\,\frac{M}{r^{2}}\,\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})`$ |     | (5.9) |

In particular, for $`M\gg\max(\frac{r^{2}}{c},r+3)`$, we have
$`\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})\gg\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})`$.

As a consequence, suppose $`D_{0}\in\Delta([K]\times[M])`$ is uniform on
a starting clique $`\{i\}\times[M]`$. For all $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, let
$`D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}`$ be the result of applying the random walk
defined in
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
for $`t`$ steps on $`D_{0}`$, and $`D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}`$ the
result of applying a simple random walk over $`G`$ for $`t`$ steps on
$`D_{0}`$. Then, for any $`\epsilon\in(0,1)`$, for
$`t_{\textup{baseline}}:=\frac{1}{2\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})}\log\frac{K}{\epsilon}`$,
$`\textup{Div}_{1}^{P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}}(D_{t_{\textup{baseline}}}^{\textup{baseline}})\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
with maximum value $`1`$. Whereas, for
$`t_{\textup{improved}}:=\frac{1}{2\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})}\log\frac{K}{\epsilon}\leq O(\frac{r^{2}}{M})\,t_{\textup{baseline}}`$,
$`\textup{Div}_{1}^{P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}}(D_{t_{\textup{improved}}}^{\textup{improved}})\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
with maximum value $`1`$.

[Proposition 5.6](#S5.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition 5.6. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that the diversity of theorem distributions generated under
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
(resp. a simple-random-walk-based conjecturer) can be guaranteed to
exceed $`1-\epsilon`$ in $`t_{\textup{improved}}`$ steps (resp.
$`t_{\textup{baseline}}`$ steps), and where
$`t_{\textup{improved}}\leq O(\frac{r^{2}}{M})\,t_{\textup{baseline}}`$.
Although this does not prove a matching lower-bound to show separation
between
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and the baseline, we believe the bounds used to derive these results are
tight so that in the worst case over all possible meta-graphs
instantiating
[Definition 5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Definition 5.5. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is $`\Theta(\frac{M}{r^{2}})`$ times more efficient than a
simple-random-walk-based conjecturer, which is substantial when the
clusters are very dense ($`M\gg r^{2}`$).

The proof of
[Proposition 5.6](#S5.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition 5.6. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Instantiating on Clustered Graphs ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
We think it is plausible that
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
improves over a baseline simple random walk $`P=P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}`$
for a broader class of clustered graphs (graphs like those depicted in
[Figure 2](#A6.F2 "In Appendix F Figures ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
than
[Definition 5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Definition 5.5. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
but we do not have a formal guarantee. Our intuition of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
on clustered graphs is that it defines a random walk that, at node
$`x`$, has a higher chance to transition to neighbors of $`x`$ in a
different cluster than $`x`$. This lets the random walk escape from its
starting cluster faster and should enable it to explore the entire
theorem graph faster.

In general, $`\tau`$ should not be set too small or too big. If
$`\tau=0`$, the diffusion embedding is not informative since every node
$`x\in V`$ is embedded as $`e_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$. If $`\tau`$ is
larger than the mixing time of $`P`$, then
$`\forall x\in V,(P^{\top})^{\tau}e_{x}\approx\pi`$, so the diffusion
embedding is also not informative. When the theorem graph is a clustered
graph consisting of equally sized clusters, there should exist a natural
setting for $`\tau`$: the number of steps it takes a random walk to
“forget" its exact starting node, where it still “remembers" its
starting cluster. More precisely, the ideal property of $`\tau`$ on a
clustered graph is that for two nodes $`x,y`$ in the same cluster, their
$`\tau`$-step random walk distributions are approximately the same:
$`p^{\tau}(x)\approx p^{\tau}(y)`$, but for $`x,y`$ in different
clusters, their $`p^{\tau}(x)`$ and $`p^{\tau}(y)`$ differ greatly.
Then, $`p^{\tau}(x)`$ serves as an identifier for which cluster $`x`$ is
in.

[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
accepts as input $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$ and a baseline reversible
conjecturer $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$, satisfying
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
It returns an improved conjecturer.
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
improves the baseline conjecturer by performing a $`\tau`$-step
look-ahead over the graph to maximize diversity. In principle, this
algorithmic scaffold can be applied to conjecturers trained empirically,
if they satisfy
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
The random walk defined by
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
may not be reversible, so the algorithmic scaffold cannot be recursively
applied to its own output.

### 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning

[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows the diffusion similarity (used in step 4 of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
can be computed via learned contrastive embeddings. A self-contained
summary of contrastive learning is in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Theorem 5.7.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a finite, undirected, connected theorem graph. Let
reversible conjecturer $`(C,P,w):=(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ satisfy
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and let $`\pi`$ be a stationary distribution for $`P`$. Let
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\subset\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(|V|)}`$ be a class
of functions from $`V`$ to $`\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$. For any
$`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, define the scale-$`\tau`$ contrastive loss of
embedding model $`h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ as:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |     |        |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}^{\tau}(h_{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{-})\sim D_{-}^{\tau}}(h_{\theta}(x)^{\top}h_{\theta}(x^{-}))^{2}-2\cdot\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{+})\sim D_{+}^{\tau}}h_{\theta}(x)^{\top}h_{\theta}(x^{+})`$ |     | (5.10) |

where $`D^{\tau}_{+},D^{\tau}_{-}\in\Delta(V\times V)`$ are
distributions of positive and negative pairs: $`(a,b)\sim D^{\tau}_{+}`$
where $`z\sim\pi,a\sim C^{\tau}(z),b\sim C^{\tau}(z)`$ ($`C^{\tau}`$
denotes applying $`C`$ $`\tau`$-times consecutively) and
$`(a,b)\sim D^{\tau}_{-}\textup{ where }a\sim\pi,b\sim\pi`$. Fix any
$`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$. Assume $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ contains a
global minimizer of $`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}^{\tau}`$ over
$`\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(|V|)}`$. For any global minimizer
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\ni h_{\theta_{*}}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$,
then
$`\forall u,v\in V,\langle p^{\tau}(u),p^{\tau}(v)\rangle_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}=h_{\theta_{*}}(u)^{\top}h_{\theta_{*}}(v)`$.

The proof of
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is in
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Main Theorems ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that the diffusion similarity of any two nodes on the graph (a
quantity computed in step 3 of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
can instead be computed from the Euclidean inner product of their
learned embeddings. Given $`n`$ samples $`\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\subset V`$
drawn i.i.d. from the stationary measure $`\pi\in\Delta(V)`$ of $`P`$,
an embedding model
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\ni h_{\hat{\theta}}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$
can be learned by computing the empirical risk minimizer (ERM,
[Definition 3.2](#S3.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 3.2 (ERM, ϵ-minimizer). ‣ Contrastive Learning. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
of the empirical contrastive loss
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$ in
[Equation B.15](#A2.E15 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Under additional assumptions, we show in
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
an end-to-end result where ERM, in a finite-sample regime with small
embedding dimension, yields embeddings that can be used to approximate
the diffusion similarity.

###### Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result).

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be any connected, undirected graph. Let $`(V,P)`$ be an
irreducible, reversible Markov chain with transition matrix
$`P\in[0,1]^{|V|\times|V|}`$ and stationary distribution
$`\pi\in\Delta(V)`$.

For any $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, instantiate the contrastive loss
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}`$ with base distribution $`\pi`$,
augmentation function $`P^{\tau}:V\to\Delta(V)`$, which augments
$`x\in V`$ into a distribution of nodes given by
$`e_{x}^{\top}P^{\tau}`$.

For any $`k\in[|V|-1]`$, let
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\subset\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}`$ be a class of
embedding models $`h_{\theta}`$ that map a domain $`V`$ into dimension
$`k`$ Euclidean space:
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}\ni h_{\theta}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}:\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}\to\mathbb{R}`$ be
the population contrastive loss, instantiated with base distribution
$`\pi`$ and augmentation function $`P^{\tau}`$, as in
[Equation B.12](#A2.E12 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}:\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}\to\mathbb{R}`$
be the empirical contrastive loss over a i.i.d. dataset of size $`n`$
drawn from $`\pi`$, as in
[Equation B.15](#A2.E15 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Assume:

1.  1.  For some $`\chi>0`$, we have that
        $`\forall h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}},\forall x\in V`$,
        $`||h_{\theta}(x)||_{\infty}\leq\chi`$.
2.  2.  $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ contains at least one global
        minimizer of $`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}`$ over
        $`\mathcal{F}_{V}^{(k)}`$ (i.e. over functions
        $`h:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$)
3.  3.  $`\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}})\leq\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}})}{n}}`$,
        where $`\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}})`$ is an
        $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$-dependent constant
4.  4.  With
        $`\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i\in[|V|]}:=\{\lambda_{i}(P^{2\tau})\}_{i\in[|V|]}`$
        being the eigenvalues of $`P^{2\tau}`$, where
        $`\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_{|V|}\geq 0`$,
        assume $`\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}>0`$.
5.  5.  There exists $`\beta>0`$ such that
        $`\forall y\in V,\,\sum_{x\in N(y)}\pi(x)\leq\beta\,\pi(y)`$. (E.g.
        if $`P`$ is the simple random walk, then $`\beta=d`$ the maximum
        degree of any node in $`G`$).

Set any $`\epsilon,\Delta\in(0,1)`$ and set
$`p_{\textup{erm fails}}=\frac{\epsilon}{\textup{poly}(k,\chi)}`$. Then,
with probability at least $`1-p_{\textup{erm fails}}`$ over the
randomness of a training dataset of size
$`n=\Theta(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}})\,\textup{poly}(k,\chi)}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{1}{p_{\textup{erm fails}}})`$
drawn i.i.d. from $`\pi`$, the following guarantee holds for any ERM
$`h_{\hat{\theta}}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ of
$`\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\textup{cont},n}`$, where
$`\textup{rank}(F_{\hat{\theta}})=\textup{rank}([\sqrt{\pi(x)}h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)^{\top}]_{x\in V})=k`$
(where $`F_{\hat{\theta}}`$ is a $`|V|\times k`$ matrix whose $`x`$-th
row is $`\sqrt{\pi(x)}h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)^{\top}`$).

|     |     |                                                                                                                                                                     |                                                                                          |                                                                                         |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\_{x\sim\pi}\Big[\exists y,z\in N(x)\cup\{x\}\,:\,                                                                                         | \phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,z)-\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h\_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle | >\frac{\lambda*{k+1}}{\pi*{\textup{min}}}+2\chi\sqrt{k}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}+\Delta\Big]`$ |     | (5.11) |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{(\beta+1)\cdot\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |                                                                                          | (5.12)                                                                                  |

[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
motivate
[Algorithm 6](#alg6 "In 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
a conjecturing algorithm that is analogous to
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
but with
[Algorithm 5](#alg5 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
replaced by a contrastive-learning procedure.

1: $`\tau\in\mathbb{N}`$, $`\eta\in[0,0.5]`$,
$`\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)`$, reversible conjecturer $`(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$
satisfying
[Definition 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1. ‣ Conjecturer. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and i.i.d. sample access to $`D\in\Delta(V)`$

2: i.i.d. sample access to $`D^{\prime}=C\#D`$

3: procedure $`C`$($`x`$)

4:   Learn an embedding function
$`h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ by minimizing the empirical
contrastive loss (e.g. via
[Algorithm 7](#alg7 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
with base distribution $`\pi`$ and augmentation function

$`x^{\prime}`$

Algorithm 6 Improved Conjecturer with Contrastive Learned Diffusion
Embeddings

Finally, we discuss how to instantiate
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
for a local subgraph of $`G`$ around the theorems of interest, rather
than needing to take $`G`$ to be the entire theorem graph, which is
impractical. For a theorem graph $`G=(V,E)`$, define the following
notion of a subgraph of $`G`$ supported on the $`T`$-neighborhood of a
node $`x\in V`$.

###### Definition 5.9 (Local Subgraph).

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a connected, undirected graph, with reversible,
nearest-neighbor-type Markov chain $`(V,P)`$. For any $`x\in V`$,
$`T\in\mathbb{N}`$, let $`G_{x,T}=(V_{x,T},E_{x,T})`$ be a subgraph of
$`G`$ supported on $`B(x,T)`$, with edges $`(a,b)`$ from $`B(x,T)\ni a`$
to $`V-B(x,T)\ni b`$ replaced by a self-loop, $`(a,a)`$ in $`G_{x,T}`$.
Let Markov chain $`(V_{x,T},P_{x,T})`$, be the restriction to $`(V,P)`$
to $`G_{x,T}`$, where any transition probability of $`(V,P)`$ along
edges from $`B(x,T)`$ to $`V-B(x,T)`$ are redirected back to their
source via the aforementioned self-loops. Let $`\pi_{x,T}`$ be its
stationary measure of $`(V_{x,T},P_{x,T})`$. For $`T\in N`$,
$`\tau\in N`$, $`y\in B(x,T)`$, denote $`p^{\tau}_{G_{x,T}}(y)`$ as the
distribution of a $`\tau`$ step random walk on $`G_{x,T}`$ according to
Markov chain $`(V_{x,T},P_{x,T})`$.

A simple observation is that: for any $`x\in V`$, on a $`T=\tau+1`$
local subgraph around $`x`$, the $`\tau`$-step random walk distribution
starting from any neighbor $`z\in N(x)`$, $`p^{\tau}_{G_{x,T}}(z)`$ is
the same as $`p^{\tau}(z)`$. In addition, for any reversible Markov
chain $`(V,P)`$ on the graph $`G`$ with stationary measure $`\pi`$, for
any $`x\in V`$ and $`T\in\mathbb{N}`$, the stationary measure
$`\pi_{x,T}`$ is equal to $`\pi`$ restricted to $`B(x,T)\subset V`$, up
to a multiplicative constant, by the self-loop construction of
$`G_{x,T}`$. Thus, the diffusion similarity computed on the local
subgraph $`G_{x,T}`$ differs from that computed on $`G`$ by a
multiplicative constant, which means the locally-computed diffusion
similarity is sufficient for solving the optimization problem in
[Equation 5.3](#S5.E3 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

To learn the spectral diffusion embedding for reversible Markov chain
$`(V,P)`$, of reversible conjecturer $`(C,P,w):=(C_{w},P_{w},w)`$ in a
local $`T`$-neighborhood around a node $`x\in V`$ via
[Algorithm 7](#alg7 "In B.1.1 Setup ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
one will require access to the following oracles, defined in
[Definition 5.9](#S5.Thmtheorem9 "Definition 5.9 (Local Subgraph). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

1.  1.  The push-forward map $`C_{x,T}:B(x,T)\to\Delta(B(x,T))`$
        representing the restricted Markov chain $`(V_{x,T},P_{x,T})`$,
        where $`\forall y\in B(x,T)`$,
        $`C_{x,T}(y)=P_{x,T}[y]\in\Delta(B(x,T))`$,
2.  2.  i.i.d. sample access to $`\pi_{x,T}\in\Delta(B(x,T))`$.

The construction of these oracles, given $`x\in V`$, $`T\in\mathbb{N}`$,
and neighbor oracle $`N:V\to 2^{V}`$ of $`G`$, is conceptually
straightforward. We describe the details of their constructions in
[Algorithm 8](#alg8 "In B.1.5 Learning Contrastive Embeddings on Local Subgraphs ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
of
[Section B.1.5](#A2.SS1.SSS5 "B.1.5 Learning Contrastive Embeddings on Local Subgraphs ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

## 6 Conclusion and Limitations

We formalized the space of theorems as a graph and a conjecturer as a
nearest-neighbor-type Markov chain over the theorem graph.
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
shows that under
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
the knowledge of the prover trained via
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
grows exponentially with the number of iterations. For the case where
[Assumption 5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
does not hold, we propose a diversity measure
([Definition 5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
for a training distribution of theorems generated by a conjecturer and
an improved conjecturing algorithm
([Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
that locally maximizes this diversity measure, by computing the
diffusion similarity
([Definition 5.4](#S5.Thmtheorem4 "Definition 5.4. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
between neighboring theorems in the theorem graph. Finally, we describe
a method to compute the diffusion similarity using contrastive learning
([Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).

One limitation of the current framework is that the conjecturer is not
adaptive toward the particular prover $`f_{t}`$ at iteration $`t`$, but
rather adaptive toward the prover class, which determines the edge set
$`E`$. It defines a time-homogeneous nearest-neighbor random walk,
whereas a time-inhomogeneous random walk would be more realistic.
Another intuition that is not captured by the current framework is that
of theorem compositionality. In particular, one can imagine a
conjecturer that has knowledge of two theorems $`X\to Y`$ and $`Y\to Z`$
may be able to conjecture $`X\to Z`$, but this is not easily compatible
with the view that a conjecturer maps a single theorem to a distribution
of theorems. More broadly, an interesting question is how to extend our
analysis to a hypergraph of theorems or dependent types [Barkeshli et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib34). Finally, we note that although this theoretical
framework is instantiated for the setting of formal theorem proving, it
could potentially serve as a framework for understanding automated
synthetic data generation for other verifiable domains besides formal
theorem proving.

## Appendix A Proof of [Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

The purpose of this section is to eventually prove
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
in
[Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

### A.1 Preliminaries.

##### Isoperimetric Inequality.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be an undirected graph with a countable set of vertices,
$`V`$, and edges $`E`$. $`G`$ is connected, and is locally finite (every
vertex has finite degree). Let $`P`$ be a Markov chain transition matrix
over $`V`$ (We will refer to the pair $`(V,P)`$ as a Markov chain). The
simple random walk is a Markov chain where every node $`x`$ transitions
uniformly to one of its neighbors in the graph,
$`N(x):=\{x^{\prime}\in V:(x,x^{\prime})\in E\}`$. In the following, we
define some basic properties of Markov chains over graphs.

For $`n\in\mathbb{N}`$, let $`p^{(n)}(x,y)`$ denote the probability the
Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ initialized at $`x`$ is at $`y`$ at the $`n`$-th
step.

###### Definition A.1.

(Irreducibility) Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ is irreducible if
$`\forall x,y\in V`$, there is some $`n\in\mathbb{N}`$ such that
$`p^{(n)}(x,y)>0`$.

For the remaining definitions, we will assume the Markov chain is
irreducible. We define aperiodicity as follows.

###### Definition A.2.

(Aperiodicity) A Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ is aperiodic if for any
$`x\in V`$, $`\textup{gcd}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}=1`$.

Note that if a Markov chain is irreducible and for some $`x\in V`$,
$`\textup{gcd}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}=1`$, then for any
$`x^{\prime}\in V`$,
$`\textup{gcd}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:p^{(n)}(x^{\prime},x^{\prime})>0\}=1`$.

A stationary measure $`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$ where
$`\pi^{\top}=\pi^{\top}P`$. If $`||\pi||_{1}=1`$, then it is a
stationary distribution. The following Theorem shows that irreducibility
and aperiodicity imply mixing for finite Markov chains.

###### Lemma A.3.

(Theorem 4.9 of \[[24](#bib.bib4)\]) Suppose that Markov chain $`(V,P)`$
is finite ($`|V|<\infty`$), irreducible and aperiodic with stationary
distribution $`\pi`$. Then there exist constants $`C>0`$ and
$`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ where

|     |                               |     |                      |
| --- | ----------------------------- | --- | -------------------- | --- | --------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\max\_{x\in V} |     | p^{(n)}(x,\cdot)-\pi |     | \_{\textup{TV}}\leq C\alpha^{n}`$ |     | (A.1) |

The following definitions introduce the notion of reversibility and
conductance.

###### Definition A.4.

(Reversibility) Let $`V`$ be an infinite, countable set. Markov chain
$`(V,P)`$ is reversible if there exists a (stationary) measure
$`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$ such that

|     |                                                                 |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\pi(x)P[x,y]=\pi(y)P[y,x]\quad\forall x,y\in V`$ |     | (A.2) |

###### Definition A.5.

(Conductance) Let $`a(x,y)=\pi(x)P[x,y]=a(y,x)`$ be the conductance
between $`x`$ and $`y`$. $`\pi(x)`$ is the total conductance at $`x`$.
For a Markov chain transition matrix $`P`$, denote its edge set $`E(P)`$
where:

|     |                                             |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle(x,y)\in E(P)\iff a(x,y)>0`$ |     | (A.3) |

Note, a nearest-neighbor-type random walk is a Markov chain $`(V,P)`$
where $`E(P)=E`$ (the edge-set of the graph $`G`$).

Now, we define the Isoperimetric Inequality for a Markov chain over a
graph, which will generalize
[Definition 3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 3.1 (Isoperimetric Inequality). ‣ Markov Chains on Graphs and Isoperimetric Inequality. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Let $`(V,P)`$ be a reversible, irreducible Markov chain with total
conductance $`\pi(\cdot)`$, edge conductance $`a(\cdot,\cdot)`$. Define
the following quantities.

|     |                             |                                                                           |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\pi(A)`$     | $`\displaystyle:=\sum_{x\in A}\pi(x),\quad\forall A\subset V`$            |     | (A.4) |
|     | $`\displaystyle a(D)`$      | $`\displaystyle:=\sum_{e\in D}a(e^{-},e^{+}),\quad\forall D\subset E(P)`$ |     | (A.5) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\partial A`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\textup{set of all edges in $E(P)$ with}`$               |     | (A.6) |
|     |                             | one endpoint in $`A`$ and the other in $`V-A`$                            |     | (A.7) |

For the definition of $`\partial A`$, note that the graphs we study in
this work are all undirected. We now define the Isoperimetric
Inequality.

###### Definition A.6 (Isoperimetric Inequality).

Let $`\mathscr{F}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}`$. A Markov chain
$`(V,P)`$ satisfies the $`\mathscr{F}`$-Isoperimetric Inequality, if
there exists a constant $`\kappa>0`$ such that for every finite
$`A\subset V`$, $`\mathscr{F}(\pi(A))\leq\kappa\,a(\partial A)`$.

The particular function $`\mathscr{F}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}`$
we care about in this work is $`\mathscr{F}(t)=t`$, corresponding to the
Strong Isoperimetric Inequality defined in
[Definition 3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 3.1 (Isoperimetric Inequality). ‣ Markov Chains on Graphs and Isoperimetric Inequality. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
However, for the proofs of some of the following Lemmas, it is useful to
define, for $`1\leq d\leq\infty`$, the $`d`$-dimensional Isoperimetric
Inequality $`\textup{IS}_{d}`$ as
[Definition A.6](#A1.Thmtheorem6 "Definition A.6 (Isoperimetric Inequality). ‣ Isoperimetric Inequality. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with $`\mathscr{F}(t)=t^{1-1/d}`$. The strong Isoperimetric Inequality
IS can be thought of as $`\textup{IS}_{d}`$ with $`d=\infty`$.

##### Hilbert Spaces and Norms.

With $`(V,P)`$ being an irreducible, reversible Markov chain with
stationary measure $`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$, let $`\ell_{0}(V)`$ denote
the linear space of finitely supported functions on $`V`$ (i.e.
functions that are non-zero only on a finite number of elements of
$`V`$). For an (undirected) edge $`e=(e^{-},e^{+})\in E`$, define the
resistance as $`r(e):=\frac{1}{a(e^{-},e^{+})}`$. The following defines
Hilbert spaces of functions, relevant to
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Definition A.7.

Define the Hilbert space $`\ell^{2}(V,\pi)`$ with inner product

|     |                                                                                   |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\langle f,g\rangle_{\ell^{2}(V,\pi)}=\sum_{v\in V}f(v)g(v)\pi(v)`$ |     | (A.8) |

$`\ell^{2}(V,\pi)`$ is the set of functions $`f:V\to\mathbb{R}`$ with
$`\sum_{v\in V}|f(v)|^{2}\pi(v)<\infty`$.

Define the Hilbert space $`\ell^{2}(V,1/\pi)`$ with inner product

|     |                                                                                               |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\langle f,g\rangle_{\ell^{2}(V,1/\pi)}=\sum_{v\in V}f(v)g(v)\frac{1}{\pi(v)}`$ |     | (A.9) |

$`\ell^{2}(V,1/\pi)`$ is the set of functions $`f:V\to\mathbb{R}`$ with
$`\sum_{v\in V}|f(v)|^{2}\frac{1}{\pi(v)}<\infty`$. When clear from
context, we will write $`\ell^{2}(\pi)`$ and $`\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$ for
$`\ell^{2}(V,\pi)`$ and $`\ell^{2}(V,1/\pi)`$, respectively.

Analogously, the Hilbert space $`\ell^{2}(E,r)`$ has inner product

|     |                                                                               |     |        |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\langle u,v\rangle_{\ell^{2}(E,r)}=\sum_{e\in E}u(e)v(e)r(e)`$ |     | (A.10) |

$`\ell^{2}(E,r)`$ is the set of functions $`f:E\to\mathbb{R}`$ with
$`\sum_{e\in E}|f(e)|^{2}r(e)<\infty`$.

We introduce the following difference operator

|     |                                                                                                         |     |        |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\nabla:\ell^{2}(V,\pi)\to\ell^{2}(E,r),\quad\nabla f(e)=\frac{f(e^{+})-f(e^{-})}{r(e)}`$ |     | (A.11) |

Define the following norms:

###### Definition A.8.

(Norms) For a function $`f:V\to\mathbb{R}`$, define its Sobolev norm

|     |                                                      |           |          |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------- | -------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle S*{P}(f):=\frac{1}{2}\sum*{x,y\in V} | f(x)-f(y) | a(x,y)`$ |     | (A.12) |

and its norm in $`\ell^{p}(V,\pi)`$

|     |                 |     |     |
| --- | --------------- | --- | --- | --- | ----------------------- | ---- | ----------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | f   |     | _{p}=\big(\sum_{x\in V} | f(x) | ^{p}\pi(x)\big)^{1/p}`$ |     | (A.13) |

whenever these sums converge. Let $`\mathcal{D(P)}`$ be the space of all
functions $`f`$ on $`V`$ such that $`\nabla f\in\ell^{2}(E,r)`$. If
$`f`$ is such a function, define its Dirichlet norm

|     |                            |                                                                     |     |        |
| --- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle D_{P}(f)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\langle\nabla f,\nabla f\rangle_{\ell^{2}(E,r)}`$   |     | (A.14) |
|     |                            | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E}\frac{(f(e^{+})-f(e^{-}))^{2}}{r(e)}`$ |     | (A.15) |
|     |                            | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in X}(f(x)-f(y))^{2}a(x,y)`$   |     | (A.16) |

##### Preliminary Lemmas.

The next few Lemmas will be used to prove
[Theorem A.14](#A1.Thmtheorem14 "Theorem A.14. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
which is key to proving the final
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Lemma A.9.

(Proposition 4.3 of \[[38](#bib.bib1)\]) Markov chain $`(V,P)`$
satisfies $`\textup{IS}_{d}`$ ($`1\leq d\leq\infty`$) if and only if

|     |                 |     |     |
| --- | --------------- | --- | --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | f   |     | _{\frac{d}{d-1}}\leq\kappa\,S_{P}(f)\quad\textup{for every $f\in\ell_{0}(V)$}`$ |     | (A.17) |

###### Proof.

See Proposition 4.3 of \[[38](#bib.bib1)\] on page 40. ∎

###### Lemma A.10.

(Lemma 2.4 of \[[38](#bib.bib1)\]) If $`f\in\mathcal{D}(P)`$, then
$`\nabla^{*}(\nabla f)=-(P-I)f`$

###### Proof.

See Lemma 2.4 of \[[38](#bib.bib1)\] on page 16. ∎

Note that $`\ell_{0}(V)\subset\mathcal{D}(P)`$.

Now, we recall some facts of linear operators. Let
$`Q=(q(i,j))_{i,j\in I}`$ be a non-negative real matrix over a countable
set. $`Q`$ acts on functions (vectors) $`I\to\mathbb{R}`$ in the usual
way by matrix multiplication on the left. Define the operator norm:

###### Definition A.11.

(Definition 2.7-1 of \[[22](#bib.bib2)\]) Let $`X,Y`$ be normed spaces
and $`Q:D(Q)\to Y`$ a linear operator, where $`D(Q)\subset X`$. $`Q`$ is
bounded if there is a real number $`c`$ s.t.

|     |                                   |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- | ------ | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\forall x\in D(Q), |     | Qx  |     | \leq c |     | x   |     | `$  |     | (A.18) |

Moreover, define $`||Q||=\sup_{x\in D(Q),x\neq 0}\frac{||Qx||}{||x||}`$

Define the adjoint of a linear operator:

###### Lemma A.12.

(Theorem 3.9-2 of \[[22](#bib.bib2)\]) The Hilbert-adjoint operator
$`Q^{*}`$ of a bounded linear operator $`Q:H_{1}\to H_{2}`$ such that

|     |                                                                    |                                           |     |        |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle Q^{*}`$                                            | $`\displaystyle:H_{2}\to H_{1}`$          |     | (A.19) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\forall x\in H_{1},y\in H_{2},\langle Qx,y\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle=\langle x,Q^{*}y\rangle`$ |     | (A.20) |

is unique and is a bounded linear operator with norm:

|     |                 |     |        |
| --- | --------------- | --- | ------ | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | Q^{\*} |     | =   |     | Q   |     | `$  |     | (A.21) |

If $`Q=Q^{*}`$, it is self-adjoint, and its operator norm has the
following Rayleigh characterization.

###### Lemma A.13.

(Theorem 9.2-2 of \[[22](#bib.bib2)\]) For any bounded, self-adjoint
$`Q`$ on a complex Hilbert space $`H`$, we have

|     |                 |     |     |
| --- | --------------- | --- | --- | --- | -------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ------------------- | --- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | Q   |     | =\sup\_{ |     | x   |     | =1} | \langle Qx,x\rangle | `$  |     | (A.22) |

###### Proof.

See Theorem 9.2-2 of \[[22](#bib.bib2)\]. ∎

##### Key Theorem.

[Theorem A.14](#A1.Thmtheorem14 "Theorem A.14. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is the key theorem which enables us to prove
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Theorem A.14.

(IS implies Spectral Expansion)

Consider an irreducible, reversible Markov chain $`(V,P)`$ that
satisfies the strong Isoperimetric inequality with Isoperimetric
constant $`\kappa`$:

|     |                                                                                                |     |        |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textup{For every finite }A\subset V,\quad\pi(A)\leq\kappa\cdot a(\partial A)`$ |     | (A.23) |

Then, the operator norm of $`P`$ in $`\ell^{2}(V,\pi)`$ is at most
$`1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$. That is,
$`||P||_{\ell^{2}(V,\pi)\to\ell^{2}(V,\pi)}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$.

###### Proof.

This follows from the proof of Theorem 10.3 of \[[38](#bib.bib1)\], but
we write it out here for completeness.

By
[Lemma A.9](#A1.Thmtheorem9 "Lemma A.9. ‣ Preliminary Lemmas. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
IS implies the Sobolev inequality $`||f||_{1}\leq\kappa\,S_{P}(f)`$ for
all $`f\in\ell_{0}(V)`$. First, we show that this implies the Dirichlet
inequality, $`||f||_{2}^{2}\leq 2\kappa^{2}D_{P}(f)`$, because:

|     |                         |                                                                                 |           |        |
| --- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------ | ----------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---- | ------------ | --- | ----------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle         |                                                                                 | f         |        | \_{2}^{4}`$ | $`\displaystyle=                          |      | f^{2}        |     | \_{1}^{2}`$ |     | (A.24) |
|     |                         | $`\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{2}S_{P}(f^{2})^{2}`$                                 |           | (A.25) |
|     |                         | $`\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{2}\big(\frac{1}{2}\sum\_{x,y\in V}a(x,y)             | f(x)-f(y) | (      | f(x)        | +                                         | f(y) | )\big)^{2}`$ |     | (A.26)      |
|     |                         | $`\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{2}D*{P}(f)\sum*{x,y\in V}a(x,y)(                     | f(x)      | +      | f(y)        | )^{2}/2`$                                 |      | (A.27)       |
|     |                         | $`\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{2}D_{P}(f)\sum_{x,y\in V}a(x,y)(f(x)^{2}+f(y)^{2})`$ |           | (A.28) |
|     |                         | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\kappa^{2}D\_{P}(f)                                        |           | f      |             | \_{2}^{2}`$                               |      | (A.29)       |
|     | $`\displaystyle\implies |                                                                                 | f         |        | \_{2}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\kappa^{2}D_{P}(f)`$ |      | (A.30)       |

By
[Lemma A.10](#A1.Thmtheorem10 "Lemma A.10. ‣ Preliminary Lemmas. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),

|     |                                                              |                                                           |     |        |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle D_{P}(f)`$                                   | $`\displaystyle=\langle f,(I-P)f\rangle_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ |     | (A.31) |
|     |                                                              | $`\displaystyle=                                          |     | f      |     | _{2}^{2}-\langle f,Pf\rangle_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}\quad\textup{for $f\in\ell_{0}(V)$}`$ |     | (A.32) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\implies\langle f,Pf\rangle_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=                                          |     | f      |     | _{2}^{2}-D_{P}(f)`$                                                               |     | (A.33) |
|     |                                                              | $`\displaystyle\leq(1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}})              |     | f      |     | ^{2}\_{2}`$                                                                       |     | (A.34) |

Where the $`||\cdot||_{2}^{2}=||\cdot||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ is the
weighted 2-norm defined in
[Definition A.8](#A1.Thmtheorem8 "Definition A.8. ‣ Hilbert Spaces and Norms. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
By
[Lemma A.13](#A1.Thmtheorem13 "Lemma A.13. ‣ Preliminary Lemmas. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),

|     |                 |                                                                                             |                                      |                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------------ | --- | ------------ | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |                                                                                             | P                                    |                                                                                                                                                                        | \_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{f\in\ell^{2}(\pi),f\neq 0}\frac{ | \langle f,Pf\rangle\_{\ell^{2}(\pi)} | }{                                                      |     | f            |     | \_{2}^{2}}`$ |     | (A.35) |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle\leq\sup\_{f\in\ell^{2}(\pi),f\neq 0}\frac{                                  | \sum\_{x,y\in V}f(x)f(y)\pi(x)P[x,y] | }{                                                                                                                                                                     |                                     | f                                                       |                                      | \_{2}^{2}}`$                                            |     | (A.36)       |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle\leq\sup*{f\in\ell^{2}(\pi),f\neq 0}\frac{\sum*{x,y\in V}\,\pi(x)P[x,y]\,    | f(x)                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        | f(y)                                | }{                                                      |                                      | f                                                       |     | \_{2}^{2}}`$ |     | (A.37)       |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{f\in\ell^{2}(\pi),f\neq 0}\frac{\langle                              | f                                    | ,P                                                                                                                                                                     | f                                   | \rangle\_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}}{                              |                                      | f                                                       |     | \_{2}^{2}}`$ |     | (A.38)       |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup*{f\in\ell^{2}(\pi),f\neq 0}\frac{\langle f,Pf\rangle*{\ell^{2}(\pi)}}{ |                                      | f                                                                                                                                                                      |                                     | \_{2}^{2}}`$                                            |                                      | (A.39)                                                  |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup*{f\in\ell*{0}(V),f\neq 0}\frac{\langle f,Pf\rangle\_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}}{  |                                      | f                                                                                                                                                                      |                                     | \_{2}^{2}}`$                                            |                                      | (Since $`\ell_{0}(V)`$ is dense in $`\ell^{2}(V,\pi)`$) |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle\leq 1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$                                               |                                      | (By [Equation A.34](#A1.E34 "In Proof. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")) |

We conclude that
$`||P||_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$,
where $`||P||_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ denotes the operator
norm of $`P`$ over $`\ell^{2}(\pi)`$.

∎

The following Corollary establishes a one-step contraction due to the
random walk according to $`P`$ on a graph satisfying IS.

###### Corollary A.15.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ and let $`(V,P)`$ be a reversible random walk on $`G`$,
with stationary measure $`\pi`$, satisfying Assumption
[5](#Thmassumption5 "Assumption 5. ‣ Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with Isoperimetric constant $`\kappa>0`$. Then, for any
$`D\in\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$, we have

|     |                 |     |           |
| --- | --------------- | --- | --------- | --- | ------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- | --- | --------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | P^{\top}D |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq(1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}) |     | D   |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.40) |

###### Proof.

The core claim is that
$`||P^{\top}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}=||P||_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$.
To see this, because $`P`$ is reversible with stationary measure
$`\pi`$, we have

|     |                                      |                                                              |     |        |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textup{diag}(\pi)P`$ | $`\displaystyle=P^{\top}\textup{diag}(\pi)`$                 |     | (A.41) |
|     | $`\displaystyle P^{\top}`$           | $`\displaystyle=\textup{diag}(\pi)P\textup{diag}(\pi)^{-1}`$ |     | (A.42) |

Thus,

|     |                 |                                        |          |            |
| --- | --------------- | -------------------------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --- | ------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------------- | --- | --------- | --- | --------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |                                        | P^{\top} |            | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{x\,:\,       |     | x                                           |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}=1} |     | P^{\top}x |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.43) |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{x\,:\,          |          | x          |                                         | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}=1}              |     | \textup{diag}(\pi)P\textup{diag}(\pi)^{-1}x |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$  |     | (A.44)    |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{x\,:\,          |          | x          |                                         | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}=1}              |     | P\textup{diag}(\pi)^{-1}x                   |     | \_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$    |     | (A.45)    |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=\sup\_{x^{\prime}\,:\, |          | x^{\prime} |                                         | \_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}=1}                |     | Px^{\prime}                                 |     | \_{\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$    |     | (A.46)    |
|     |                 | $`\displaystyle=                       |          | P          |                                         | \_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}`$ |     | (A.47)                                      |

[Equation A.46](#A1.E46 "In Proof. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
follows from the fact that for any
$`x\in\ell^{2}(1/\pi),x^{\prime}=\textup{diag}(\pi)^{-1}x\in\ell^{2}(\pi)`$.
Conversely, for any $`x^{\prime}\in\ell^{2}(\pi)`$,
$`x=\textup{diag}(\pi)x^{\prime}\in\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$.

Finally, by
[Theorem A.14](#A1.Thmtheorem14 "Theorem A.14. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
$`||P||_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}`$.
Since
$`||P||_{\ell^{2}(\pi)\to\ell^{2}(\pi)}=||P^{\top}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$,
then for any $`D\in\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$, we have

|     |                 |     |           |
| --- | --------------- | --- | --------- | --- | ----------------------- | --- | -------- | --- | --------------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- | --- | --------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | P^{\top}D |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq |     | P^{\top} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)\to\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\, |     | D   |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq(1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}) |     | D   |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.48) |

∎

### A.2 Proof of [Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

See
[4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 4.2 (Analysis of ). ‣ 4.3 Expansion Guarantee for . ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

We reason inductively, by analyzing the behavior of
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
each iteration.

First, suppose at iteration $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$,
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
has i.i.d. sample access to $`D_{t}\in\Delta(V)`$, and trains prover
$`f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ to where
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$
(an event which occurs with probability at least $`1-\delta`$ according
to
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
(using the subroutine,
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
generates $`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$ from $`D_{t}`$ and then generates $`D_{t+1}`$
from $`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$ by filtering out theorems whose pass rate is below
$`p/2`$. By
[Corollary A.15](#A1.Thmtheorem15 "Corollary A.15. ‣ Key Theorem. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),

|     |                 |     |              |
| --- | --------------- | --- | ------------ | --- | ------------------------- | --- | ---------------- | --- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | ------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | C*{w}\#D*{t} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}:= |     | (P^{\top})D\_{t} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}\leq(1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}})^{2} |     | D\_{t} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.49) |

Under the event that
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
let

|     |                             |                                                                                          |     |        |
| --- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle\alpha_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim C_{w}\#D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2]`$ |     | (A.50) |
|     |                             | $`\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p]`$        |     | (A.51) |
|     |                             | $`\displaystyle\geq 1-\epsilon`$                                                         |     | (A.52) |

Let $`D_{t+1}`$ be a new distribution whose sampling process involves
sampling $`x\sim C_{w}\#D_{t}`$ until
$`\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2`$ and then returning such an
$`x`$ (i.e. the rejection sampling step in
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
This process provides i.i.d. sample access to $`D_{t+1}`$ supported on
the $`\alpha_{t}`$-fraction of theorems in $`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$ where
$`\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2`$. The probability of any theorem
under $`D_{t+1}`$ is equal to its respective probability under
$`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$ multiplied by
$`\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\leq\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}`$. Since for
$`f\in\ell^{2}(1/\pi)`$,
$`||f||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}=\sum_{v\in V}|f(v)|^{2}\frac{1}{\pi(v)}`$,
then

|     |                 |     |          |
| --- | --------------- | --- | -------- | --- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------------ | --- | ------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | D\_{t+1} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq(\frac{1}{1-\epsilon})^{2} |     | C*{w}\#D*{t} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.53) |

Combining with
[Equation A.49](#A1.E49 "In Proof. ‣ A.2 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
we conclude

|     |                 |     |          |
| --- | --------------- | --- | -------- | --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | ------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | D\_{t+1} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}\leq(\frac{1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}}{1-\epsilon})^{2} |     | D\_{t} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}`$ |     | (A.54) |

We now describe how these per-iteration guarantees can be put together
inductively. We claim the following iteration invariant: for every
iteration $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, conditional on the event that all previous
iterations did not fail, then
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
has access to a theorem distribution $`D_{t}`$ satisfying the premise of
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
that $`\forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_{t}),`$ the proof of $`x`$ is
known. Moreover, the $`t`$th iteration fails with probability at most
$`\delta`$.

As the base case,
[Assumption 1](#Thmassumption1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
ensures
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
has i.i.d. sample access to cold-start theorem distribution $`D_{0}`$,
and that all proofs of theorems in $`\operatorname{supp}(D_{0})`$ are
known. The iteration invariant holds.

Regarding the inductive step, suppose at iteration $`t`$, the algorithm
has i.i.d. sample access to $`D_{t}`$, where for all
$`x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_{t})`$, the proof of $`x`$ is known. Suppose
also that all previous iterations $`\{0\}\cup[t-1]`$ did not fail. By
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
can train a new prover $`f_{t}`$ using i.i.d. sample access to
$`D_{t}`$, which guarantees that
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$
with failure probability at most $`\delta`$. By
[Assumption 3](#Thmassumption3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$
implies that
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim C_{w}\#D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2]\geq 1-\epsilon`$.
The rejection sampling procedure in
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
which generates $`D_{t+1}`$ from $`C_{w}\#D_{t}`$, ensures that
$`\forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_{t+1})`$,
$`\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2`$, so that it is efficient to
sample the proof of any theorem in $`\operatorname{supp}(D_{t+1})`$ from
$`f_{t}`$. Thus, the proof of every theorem in
$`\operatorname{supp}(D_{t+1})`$ is known, and $`D_{t+1}`$ satisfies the
premise of
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
This iteration fails with probability at most $`\delta`$, which occurs
if step that trains $`f_{t}`$ from $`D_{t}`$ fails.

Thus, by induction over the iteration number $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, we
conclude from
[Equation A.54](#A1.E54 "In Proof. ‣ A.2 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
that for every $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, conditional on the event that every
iteration $`i\in\{0\}\cup[t-1]`$ does not fail (which occurs with
probability at least $`1-t\,\delta`$ since each iteration fails with
probability at most $`\delta`$), then

|     |                 |     |        |
| --- | --------------- | --- | ------ | --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | ------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle |     | D\_{t} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}\leq(\frac{1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}}{1-\epsilon})^{2t} |     | D\_{0} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |     | (A.55) |

Finally,
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Prover-Conjecturer System. ‣ 4.2 Random-Walk Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
trains the final prover $`f_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ on
$`D_{t}`$ at iteration $`t`$. With failure probability at most
$`\delta`$, we have
$`D_{t}(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p\})\geq 1-\epsilon`$.

At iteration $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, suppose none of the training guarantees
of the $`t+1`$ provers $`\{f_{0},f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}\}`$ fail, which
occurs with probability at least $`1-(t+1)\,\delta`$. Applying
[Lemma E.1](#A5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma E.1. ‣ Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with $`D^{\prime}=D_{t}`$,
$`A^{\prime}=\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p\}`$ and the
guarantee that
$`D_{t}(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p\})\geq 1-\epsilon`$,
we have

|     |                 |                                                |                                                                 |
| --- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | -------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle | \{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f\_{t})\geq p\} | \geq\frac{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}{\sup\_{z\in V}\pi(z)}\cdot\frac{1}{ |     | D\_{t} |     | ^{2}\_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}`$ |     | (A.56) |

By
[Equation A.55](#A1.E55 "In Proof. ‣ A.2 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
the conclusion follows.

|     |                 |                                                |                                                         |
| --- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ |
|     | $`\displaystyle | \{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f\_{t})\geq p\} | \geq\frac{(1-\epsilon)^{2}}{(\sup\_{z\in V}\pi(z))\cdot |     | D\_{0} |     | \_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}}\cdot(\frac{1-\epsilon}{1-\frac{1}{2\kappa^{2}}})^{2t}.`$ |     | (A.57) |

Note also that since
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim C_{w}\#D_{t}}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f_{t})\geq p/2]\geq 1-\epsilon`$
at iteration $`t`$, the probability of rejection each iteration is at
most $`\epsilon`$, so that the rejection sampling procedure per
iteration is fairly efficient. However, the probability of rejection
compounds over iterations, so that the expected number of samples from
$`D_{0}`$ needed to sample from $`D_{t}`$ is proportional to
$`(\frac{1}{1-\epsilon})^{t}`$.

∎

## Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning

The purpose of this section is to show the connection between
contrastive learning and diffusion similarity, and show how an embedding
model learned by minimizing a contrastive loss can be used to compute
the diffusion similarity (and diffusion distance) between points on a
graph. Our main results, in
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Main Theorems ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
include
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
an infinite-sample and large embedding dimension learning result, and
[Theorem 5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
a finite-sample and small embedding dimension learning result.

### B.1 Preliminary Lemmas

#### B.1.1 Setup

Contrastive learning defines an algorithm for learning an embedding
model that maps elements from a domain $`V`$ (e.g. the set of real-world
images) into Euclidean space $`\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ for some
$`k\in\mathbb{N}`$. It is most notably used for training neural networks
as embedding models, and we let $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ denote
the hypothesis class of models $`h_{\theta}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ which
we assume contains the ground-truth embedding model that we must learn.
The core idea of contrastive learning is to define two distributions of
pairs of elements in $`V`$: a positive pair distribution
$`D_{+}\in\Delta(V\times V)`$ , and a negative pair distribution
$`D_{-}\in\Delta(V\times V)`$. Given i.i.d. samples from both
distributions, the trained model is encouraged to embed two elements
sampled from a positive pair $`(x,y)\sim D_{+}`$ close together in
Euclidean space, while embedding two elements sampled from a negative
pair $`(x,x^{\prime})\sim D_{-}`$ far apart in Euclidean space. These
two distributions of pairs of elements are used to define a contrastive
loss, and training the model amounts to minimizing an empirical estimate
of the contrastive loss from finite samples.

In fact, contrastive learning can be described mathematically through
the lens of matrix factorization, as articulated in \[[17](#bib.bib6)\].
The benefit of this viewpoint of contrastive learning is that it enables
us to provably characterize the learned embeddings and the sample
complexity of learning them. In the following, we will describe and use
the mathematical setup for contrastive learning of \[[17](#bib.bib6)\].

Let the domain $`V`$ consist of $`N\in\mathbb{N}`$ elements, where $`N`$
is large but finite. We will identify $`V`$ with $`[N]`$ here for
simplicity. Define $`\mu\in\Delta([N])`$ as the base distribution and
$`Q\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}`$ as an augmentation scheme. Alternatively,
overloading notation, we can view $`Q:[N]\to\Delta(N)`$ as a mapping
from an element $`x`$ to a distribution over augmentations of $`x`$,
$`Q(x)`$. For every $`x\in[N]`$, this distribution of augmentations,
$`Q(x)`$, equals the $`x`$-th row of the matrix-representation of $`Q`$.

We will first introduce the matrix factorization viewpoint of
contrastive learning, and we will from this how to define the positive
and negative pair distributions $`D_{+},D_{-}\in\Delta([N]\times[N])`$
from $`\mu`$ and $`Q`$ and the final learning algorithm. Let
$`A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}`$ and its normalization $`\overline{A}`$ be
positive semi-definite (p.s.d.) matrices of the form,

|     |                               |                                                   |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle A`$           | $`\displaystyle=Q^{\top}\,\textup{diag}(\mu)\,Q`$ |     | (B.1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle D`$           | $`\displaystyle=\textup{diag}(A\mathbf{1})`$      |     | (B.2) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\overline{A}`$ | $`\displaystyle=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}`$               |     | (B.3) |

For rank-$`k`$ factor $`F_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times k}`$, let
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textup{mf}}(F_{\theta}):=||\overline{A}-F_{\theta}F_{\theta}^{\top}||_{F}^{2}`$
be the matrix factorization loss for matrix
$`\overline{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}`$ be the class of embedding models. We will
parameterize $`F_{\theta}`$ by an embedding model
$`h_{\theta}:[N]\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$. Towards this, if we let
$`\sigma_{xy}`$ denote the $`(x,y)`$-th entry of $`A`$,

|     |                                           |                                              |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle A`$                       | $`\displaystyle=[\sigma_{xy}]_{x,y\in[N]}`$  |     | (B.4) |
