### B.2 Main Theorems

See
[5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

By
[Lemma B.6](#A2.Thmtheorem6 "Lemma B.6 (Global Minimizers for Contrastive Loss). ‣ B.1.3 The Connection Between Diffusion Embeddings and Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
there exists an orthogonal matrix $`R\in O^{|V|\times|V|}`$ where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall u\in V,h_{\theta_{*}}(u)=R\,\Phi_{\tau}(u)\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}`$ |  | (B.116) |

Thus,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall u,v\in V,\langle h_{\theta_{*}}(u),h_{\theta_{*}}(v)\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle=\langle R\,\Phi_{\tau}(u),R\,\Phi_{\tau}(v)\rangle`$ |  | (B.117) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\langle\Phi_{\tau}(u),\Phi_{\tau}(v)\rangle`$ |  | (B.118) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\langle p^{\tau}(u),p^{\tau}(v)\rangle_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}`$ |  | (By [Lemma B.4](#A2.Thmtheorem4 "Lemma B.4 (Diffusion Embeddings). ‣ B.1.3 The Connection Between Diffusion Embeddings and Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")) |

∎

Below is our end-to-end learning result, which can be viewed as a
finite-sample, small-embedding dimension version of
[Theorem 5.7](#S5.Thmtheorem7 "Theorem 5.7. ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

See
[5.8](#S5.Thmtheorem8 "Theorem 5.8 (End-to-End Contrastive Learning Result). ‣ 5.3 Computing Diffusion Similarity via Contrastive Learning ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

By
[Lemma B.2](#A2.Thmtheorem2 "Lemma B.2 (Generalization of ERM). ‣ B.1.2 Lemmas on Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
with probability at least $`1-p_{\textup{erm fails}}`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}(h_{\hat{\theta}})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}_{\textup{cont}}(h_{\theta_{*}})+\epsilon`$ |  | (B.119) |
|  | $`\displaystyle||\overline{A}-F_{\hat{\theta}}F_{\hat{\theta}}^{\top}||^{2}_{F}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq||\overline{A}-F_{\theta_{*}}F_{\theta_{*}}^{\top}||^{2}_{F}+\epsilon`$ |  | (B.120) |

Under that event, since $`\textup{rank}(F_{\hat{\theta}})=k`$ by
assumption, by
[Lemma B.11](#A2.Thmtheorem11 "Lemma B.11 (Approximate minimizers are close to a global minimizer). ‣ B.1.4 Matrix Factorization Lemmas ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
and
[Lemma B.12](#A2.Thmtheorem12 "Lemma B.12. ‣ B.1.4 Matrix Factorization Lemmas ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi}||h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(x)||_{2}^{2}\leq\epsilon\cdot\frac{\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |  | (B.121) |

Where we’ve used that
$`||\overline{A}||_{2}=\lambda_{1}(\overline{A})=\lambda_{1}(P^{2\tau})=1`$.
By Markov’s inequality,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\pi}\Big[||h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(x)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |  | (B.122) |

In fact, using the premise that
$`\exists\beta>0\,:\forall y\in V,\,\sum_{x\in N(y)}\pi(x)\leq\beta\,\pi(y)`$,
we can extend this closeness guarantee to a neighborhood around
$`x\sim\pi`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\pi}\Big[\exists y\in N(x):||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.123) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi}\sum_{y\in N(x)}1\Big[||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.124) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in V}\pi(x)\sum_{y\in N(x)}1\Big[||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.125) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\sum_{y\in V}\beta\,\pi(y)\,1\Big[||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.126) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\beta\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi}\Big[||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.127) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\beta\cdot\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |  | (B.128) |

Thus,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\pi}\Big[\exists y\in N(x):||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\textup{ or }||h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(x)||_{2}^{2}\geq\Delta\Big]`$ |  | (B.129) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{(\beta+1)\cdot\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |  | (B.130) |

Under the event that $`x\sim\pi`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall y\in N(x):||h_{\hat{\theta}}(y)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y)||_{2}^{2}\leq\Delta\textup{ and }||h_{\hat{\theta}}(x)-R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(x)||_{2}^{2}\leq\Delta`$ |  | (B.131) |

Then, $`\forall y,z\in N(x)\cup\{x\}`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\langle R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(y),R\,h_{\theta_{*}}(z)\rangle+2\max_{h_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{emb}}}\max_{\hat{y}\in V}||h_{\theta}(\hat{y})||_{2}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}+\Delta`$ |  | (B.132) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\langle h_{\theta_{*}}(y),h_{\theta_{*}}(z)\rangle+2\chi\sqrt{k}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}+\Delta`$ |  | (B.133) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\textup{Similarly, }\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\langle h_{\theta_{*}}(y),h_{\theta_{*}}(z)\rangle-2\chi\sqrt{k}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}-\Delta`$ |  | (B.134) |

By
[Lemma B.6](#A2.Thmtheorem6 "Lemma B.6 (Global Minimizers for Contrastive Loss). ‣ B.1.3 The Connection Between Diffusion Embeddings and Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
(which says
$`\langle h_{\theta_{*}}(x),h_{\theta_{*}}(y)\rangle=\langle\Phi_{t}^{\leq k}(x),\Phi_{t}^{\leq k}(y)\rangle`$)
and
[Lemma B.5](#A2.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma B.5. ‣ B.1.3 The Connection Between Diffusion Embeddings and Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
then $`\forall x,y\in V`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\Phi_{t}(x),\Phi_{t}(y)\rangle-\frac{\lambda_{k+1}}{\pi_{\textup{min}}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\langle h_{\theta_{*}}(x),h_{\theta_{*}}(y)\rangle\leq\langle\Phi_{t}(x),\Phi_{t}(y)\rangle+\frac{\lambda_{k+1}}{\pi_{\textup{min}}}`$ |  | (B.135) |

It follows that when $`x\sim\pi`$ satisfies
[Equation B.131](#A2.E131 "In Proof. ‣ B.2 Main Theorems ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
then with
$`\xi:=\frac{\lambda_{k+1}}{\pi_{\textup{min}}}+2\chi\sqrt{k}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}+\Delta`$,
we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\Phi_{t}(y),\Phi_{t}(z)\rangle-\xi`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle\leq\langle\Phi_{t}(y),\Phi_{t}(z)\rangle+\xi`$ |  | (B.136) |

Since by
[Lemma B.4](#A2.Thmtheorem4 "Lemma B.4 (Diffusion Embeddings). ‣ B.1.3 The Connection Between Diffusion Embeddings and Contrastive Learning ‣ B.1 Preliminary Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
we have
$`\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,z)=\langle\Phi_{t}(y),\Phi_{t}(z)\rangle`$,
then with
$`\xi:=\frac{\lambda_{k+1}}{\pi_{\textup{min}}}+2\chi\sqrt{k}\cdot\sqrt{\Delta}+\Delta`$,
we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\pi}\Big[\exists y,z\in N(x)\cup\{x\}\,:\,|\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,z)-\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle|>\xi\Big]`$ |  | (B.137) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{(\beta+1)\cdot\Big(1+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k+1}^{2}}}\Big)^{2}}{2(\sqrt{2}-1)\lambda_{k}}`$ |  | (B.138) |

In short, for sufficiently small $`\epsilon`$, the learned embedding
model $`h_{\hat{\theta}}:V\to\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ can be used to approximate
$`\phi^{\textup{diff}}_{\tau}(y,z)`$ of neighboring points of most
$`x\in V`$ by the inner product,
$`\langle h_{\hat{\theta}}(y),h_{\hat{\theta}}(z)\rangle`$.

∎

## Appendix C Instantiating [Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms") on Clustered Graphs

In this section, we first describe a concrete end-to-end result for how
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
improves over a simple random walk, in terms of diversity
([Definition 5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
on a special class of clustered graphs.

### C.1 End-to-End Result of [Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms") on Clique Graphs

[Proposition 5.6](#S5.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition 5.6. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is an end-to-end result for
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
showing that on a special class of theorem graphs
([Definition 5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Definition 5.5. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")),
that
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
explores the graph faster than a simple random walk. The final guarantee
is in terms of the spectral gaps of the random walks, and the diversity
of the distributions they generate, according to
[Definition 5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 5.2 (Diversity Measure). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

See
[5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Definition 5.5. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

See
[5.6](#S5.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition 5.6. ‣ 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

Fix a node $`x=(i,a)\in C_{i}`$. Its neighbors split into two classes:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle I_{x}`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\{(i,b):b\in[M],\ b\neq a\}`$ |  | (C.1) |
|  | $`\displaystyle E_{x}`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\{(j,a):j\in N_{Q}(i)\},`$ |  | (C.2) |

with $`|I_{x}|=M-1`$, $`|E_{x}|=r`$, and total degree $`d=M-1+r.`$ For
$`\tau=1`$, since $`G`$ is $`d`$-regular,
$`\forall x,p^{1}(x)=\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}_{N(x)}`$. The matrix
$`M_{x}^{\prime}`$ in
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
equals, up to a constant multiplicative factor of $`d^{-3}`$,
$`M_{x}^{\prime}[y,z]\propto|N(y)\cap N(z)|,y,z\in N(x).`$ Therefore
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
minimizes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle F_{x}(\mu):=\sum_{y,z\in N(x)}\mu(y)\mu(z)\,|N(y)\cap N(z)|\qquad\text{over }\mu\in\Delta(N(x)).`$ |  | (C.3) |

Write $`u_{b}:=(i,b)\in I_{x}`$ and $`v_{j}:=(j,a)\in E_{x}.`$ We
compute the relevant neighborhood intersections.

##### (i) Internal/internal.

For any $`b\in[M],b\neq a`$, $`|N(u_{b})\cap N(u_{b})|=d.`$ For any
distinct $`b,b^{\prime}\neq a`$,
$`|N(u_{b})\cap N(u_{b^{\prime}})|=M-2.`$ Indeed, $`u_{b}`$ and
$`u_{b^{\prime}}`$ share exactly the $`M-2`$ vertices in $`C_{i}`$ other
than $`u_{b}`$ and $`u_{b^{\prime}}`$.

##### (ii) Internal/external.

For any $`b\neq a`$ and any $`j\in N_{Q}(i)`$,
$`|N(u_{b})\cap N(v_{j})|=2.`$ The two common neighbors are $`x=(i,a)`$
and $`(j,b)`$.

##### (iii) External/external.

For any $`j\in N_{Q}(i)`$, $`|N(v_{j})\cap N(v_{j})|=d.`$ For any
distinct $`j,k\in N_{Q}(i)`$, $`|N(v_{j})\cap N(v_{k})|=c.`$ Indeed, the
common neighbors are exactly the vertices
$`\{(\ell,a):\ell\in N_{Q}(j)\cap N_{Q}(k)\}`$ whose number is $`c`$ by
assumption.

Now let
$`\mu_{b}:=\mu(u_{b}),\,\,\nu_{j}:=\mu(v_{j}),\,\,s:=\sum_{b\neq a}\mu_{b}.`$
Then $`\sum_{j\in N_{Q}(i)}\nu_{j}=1-s`$, and the objective becomes

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle F_{x}(\mu)`$ | $`\displaystyle=d\sum_{b\neq a}\mu_{b}^{2}+(M-2)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b,b^{\prime}\neq a\\
b\neq b^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\mu_{b}\mu_{b^{\prime}}+d\sum_{j\in N_{Q}(i)}\nu_{j}^{2}+c\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,k\in N_{Q}(i)\\
j\neq k\end{subarray}}\nu_{j}\nu_{k}+2\cdot\sum_{j\in N_{Q}(i),\,b\neq a}\nu_{j}\mu_{b}`$ |  | (C.4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\bigl(d-(M-2)\bigr)\sum_{b\neq a}\mu_{b}^{2}+(M-2)s^{2}+(d-c)\sum_{j\in N_{Q}(i)}\nu_{j}^{2}+c(1-s)^{2}+2\cdot 2s(1-s)`$ |  | (C.5) |

Since $`d-(M-2)=r+1>0,\,d-c>0,`$ for fixed $`s`$ the objective is
minimized by taking $`\mu_{b}`$ uniform on $`I_{x}`$ and $`\nu_{j}`$
uniform on $`E_{x}`$, i.e.

|     |                          |                                 |     |       |
|-----|--------------------------|---------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     | $`\displaystyle\mu_{b}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{s}{M-1}`$ |     | (C.6) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\nu_{j}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1-s}{r}`$ |     | (C.7) |

Thus it suffices to minimize the one-variable quadratic

|     |                                                              |     |       |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     | $`\displaystyle f_{M}(s)=A_{M}s^{2}+4s(1-s)+B_{M}(1-s)^{2}`$ |     | (C.8) |

where $`A_{M}=M-2+\frac{r+1}{M-1}`$ and $`B_{M}=c+\frac{d-c}{r}.`$
Expanding,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle f_{M}(s)=(A_{M}+B_{M}-4)s^{2}+(4-2B_{M})s+B_{M}.`$ |  | (C.9) |

Because $`M\geq 3`$, we have $`A_{M}+B_{M}-4>0`$, so $`f_{M}`$ has the
unique minimizer

|     |                                                              |     |        |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|--------|
|     | $`\displaystyle s=\eta_{M}:=\frac{B_{M}-2}{A_{M}+B_{M}-4}.`$ |     | (C.10) |

Hence the unique optimizer of
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
at $`x=(i,a)`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mu_{x}^{*}=\frac{\eta_{M}}{M-1}\sum_{b\neq a}e_{(i,b)}+\frac{1-\eta_{M}}{r}\sum_{j\in N_{Q}(i)}e_{(j,a)}`$ |  | (C.11) |

In particular,
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
sends total mass $`\eta_{M}`$ to the current cluster $`C_{i}`$, and
total mass $`(1-\eta_{M})/r`$ to each neighboring cluster $`C_{j}`$,
$`j\in N_{Q}(i)`$. These transition dynamics depend only on the cluster
index $`i`$, not on the label $`a`$. Thus, we can describe the dynamics
of the Markov chain in terms of cluster-level transition probabilities,
i.e. as a random walk over the meta-graph $`Q`$, where each cluster
$`\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}`$ corresponds to one state. As a random walk over
the meta-graph $`Q`$,
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is described by a transition matrix
$`P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}\in[0,1]^{K\times K}.`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}=\eta_{M}I_{K}+(1-\eta_{M})P_{Q}\in[0,1]^{K\times K}`$ |  | (C.12) |

Similarly, the simple random walk on $`G`$ can also be described as a
random walk over the meta-graph $`Q`$, whose transition matrix we denote
$`P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}\in[0,1]^{K\times K}`$. From any
$`x=(i,a)\in C_{i}`$ there are $`M-1`$ neighbors inside $`C_{i}`$ and
exactly one neighbor in $`C_{j}`$ for each $`j\in N_{Q}(i)`$. Therefore,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}=\frac{M-1}{M-1+r}I_{K}+\frac{r}{M-1+r}P_{Q}\in[0,1]^{K\times K}`$ |  | (C.13) |

Regarding notation, define
$`P_{\textup{baseline}}\in[0,1]^{KM\times KM}`$ and
$`P_{\textup{improved}}\in[0,1]^{KM\times KM}`$ as the simple random
walk over $`G`$ and the random walk induced by
[Algorithm 4](#alg4 "In 5.2 Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
over $`G`$ (not over the meta-graph $`Q`$), respectively.
$`P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}`$ and $`P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}`$ are
the meta-graph analogs of $`P_{\textup{baseline}}`$ and
$`P_{\textup{improved}}.`$

Additionally, for transition matrix $`P`$ of a Markov chain, define the
spectral gap as $`\gamma(P):=1-\max(\lambda_{2}(P),|\lambda_{K}(P)|)`$.
Then,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-\lambda_{2}(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})`$ |  | (Since when $`M-1\geq r,`$ then $`P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}\succeq 0`$) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=1-[\frac{M-1}{M-1+r}+\frac{r}{M-1+r}\lambda_{2}(P_{Q})]`$ |  | (C.14) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{r}{M-1+r}(1-\lambda_{2}(P_{Q}))`$ |  | (C.15) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\min\big(1-\lambda_{2}(\eta_{M}I+(1-\eta_{M})P_{Q}),1-|\lambda_{K}(\eta_{M}I+(1-\eta_{M})P_{Q})|\big)`$ |  | (C.16) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\min\big((1-\eta_{M})(1-\lambda_{2}(P_{Q})),1-|\lambda_{K}(\eta_{M}I+(1-\eta_{M})P_{Q})|\big)`$ |  | (C.17) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\min\big((1-\eta_{M})(1-\lambda_{2}(P_{Q})),1-|2\eta_{M}-1|\big)`$ |  | (Since $`\lambda_{K}(P_{Q})\geq-1`$) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\implies\frac{\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})}{\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{M-1+r}{r}\min(1-\eta_{M},\frac{1-|2\eta_{M}-1|}{1-\lambda_{2}(P_{Q})})`$ |  | (C.18) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{M-1+r}{r}\min(1-\eta_{M},\frac{1-|2\eta_{M}-1|}{2})`$ |  | ($`1-\lambda_{2}(P_{Q})\leq 2`$) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{M-1+r}{r}\min(1-\eta_{M},\eta_{M})`$ |  | (C.19) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{M-1+r}{r}\cdot\frac{c+\frac{d-c}{r}-2}{M-2+\frac{r+1}{M-1}+c+\frac{d-c}{r}-4}`$ |  | (C.20) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\Omega(\frac{M}{r^{2}})`$ |  | (C.21) |

This proves the first claim.

Towards the second claim, by assumption, $`D_{0}`$ is uniform over its
starting cluster:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall a,a^{\prime}\in[M],\forall i\in[K],D_{0}((i,a))=D_{0}((i,a^{\prime}))`$ |  | (C.22) |

By an inductive argument we have that for all
$`t\in\mathbb{N},D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}`$ and
$`D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}`$ are uniform over clusters:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall a,a^{\prime}\in[M],\forall i\in[K],D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}((i,a))`$ | $`\displaystyle=D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}((i,a^{\prime}))\textup{ and }`$ |  | (C.23) |
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}((i,a))`$ | $`\displaystyle=D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}((i,a^{\prime}))`$ |  | (C.24) |

Thus, for all $`t\in\mathbb{N}`$, $`D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}`$ (resp.
$`D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}`$) is characterized by a probability
distribution $`q_{t}^{\textup{improved}}\in\Delta([K])`$ (resp.
$`q_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}`$) over clusters, where each node in cluster
$`i`$ has probability $`\frac{q_{t}^{\textup{improved}}(i)}{M}`$ (resp.
$`\frac{q_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}(i)}{M}`$). The stationary measure
$`\pi`$ is uniform over the $`KM`$ nodes of $`G`$ since $`G`$ is
regular. Thus,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall t\in\mathbb{N},||D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=KM\cdot\frac{1}{M}\cdot||q_{t}^{\textup{improved}}||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.25) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall t\in\mathbb{N},||D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=KM\cdot\frac{1}{M}\cdot||q_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.26) |

Let $`u=\frac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}`$ be the stationary measure of both
$`P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}`$ and $`P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}`$,
random walks over the meta-graph $`Q`$. With $`\tau=1`$ and setting
$`P:=P_{\textup{s.r.w.}}=P_{\textup{baseline}}`$, for any
$`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ we have:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall t\in\mathbb{N},||D_{t}^{\textup{improved}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1+K\cdot||q_{t}^{\textup{improved}}-u||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.27) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\implies\forall t\in\mathbb{N},\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t}^{\textup{improved}})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{||(D_{t}^{\textup{improved}})^{\top}P_{\textup{baseline}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.28) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+K\cdot||(q_{t}^{\textup{improved}}-u)^{\top}P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}||_{2}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.29) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+K\cdot||(q_{0}-u)^{\top}(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})^{t}P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}||_{2}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.30) |

For
$`t=\frac{1}{2\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})}\log\frac{K}{\epsilon}`$,
then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle K\,||(q_{0}-u)^{\top}(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})^{t}P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.31) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq K\,[(1-\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}))^{t}(1-\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}))]^{2}||q_{0}-u||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.32) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq K\,(1-\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)}))^{2t}`$ |  | (C.33) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\epsilon`$ |  | (C.34) |

Since $`\epsilon<1`$, when
$`t=\frac{1}{2\gamma(P_{\textup{improved}}^{(Q)})}\log\frac{K}{\epsilon}`$,
we have that
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t}^{\textup{improved}})\geq\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon`$.

By an analogous argument for $`D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}`$, for any
$`t\in\mathbb{N}`$ we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall t\in\mathbb{N},||D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1+K\cdot||q_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}-u||_{2}^{2}`$ |  | (C.35) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\implies\forall t\in\mathbb{N},\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{||(D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}})^{\top}P_{\textup{baseline}}||_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.36) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+K\cdot||(q_{t}^{\textup{baseline}}-u)^{\top}P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}||_{2}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.37) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+K\cdot||(q_{0}-u)^{\top}(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})^{t}P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)}||_{2}^{2}}`$ |  | (C.38) |

For
$`t=\frac{1}{2\gamma(P_{\textup{baseline}}^{(Q)})}\log\frac{K}{\epsilon}`$,
then
$`\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D_{t}^{\textup{baseline}})\geq\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon`$.

∎

## Appendix D Justification of [Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

The core result of this section is
[Lemma D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Finer-Grained Assumptions). ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
which justifies
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
by showing that finer-grained assumptions inspired from statistical
learning theory implies
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

###### Lemma D.1 (Finer-Grained Assumptions).

Assumptions
[6](#Thmassumption6 "Assumption 6. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
[7](#Thmassumption7 "Assumption 7. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
[8](#Thmassumption8 "Assumption 8. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
imply Assumption
[2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Primitive Assumptions ‣ 4 Framework and Random-Exploration Baseline ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").

### D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions

First, we introduce Assumptions
[6](#Thmassumption6 "Assumption 6. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms") -
[8](#Thmassumption8 "Assumption 8. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
Let $`\textup{Ver}:V\times\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}`$ be a formal verifier
where for theorem $`x\in V`$, then $`\textup{Ver}(x,y)=1`$ iff
$`y\in\{0,1\}^{*}`$ is a correct proof of $`x`$. The first assumption
assumes the function class $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ of provers
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}\ni f:V\to\Delta(\{0,1\}^{*})`$ can
express the ground-truth function.

###### Assumption 6.

(Expressivity) There exists $`f^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$
which is a ground-truth prover, so that for every theorem $`x\in V,`$
$`f^{*}(x)\in\Delta(\{0,1\}^{*})`$ is distribution over correct proofs
of $`x`$.

Each $`f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ maps a theorem to a
distribution of proofs ($`f:V\to\Delta(\{0,1\}^{*})`$, where $`V`$ is
the set of theorems). Thus we can define a notion of the success rate of
a prover on a theorem as the probability that the prover outputs a
correct proof. Formally, let $`f(x,r)`$ be the output of prover $`f`$ on
theorem $`x`$ and random seed $`r`$, where $`r\sim D_{r}`$. Define the
following loss function over $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ (which
abstracts away the randomness $`r\sim D_{r}`$ into a success rate):

###### Definition D.2.

(Loss Functions) Define the following loss functions on provers in
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\ell(f,x)`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim D_{r}}[1-\textup{Ver}(x,f(x,r))]`$ |  | (D.1) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=1-\operatorname{succ}(x,f)`$ |  | (D.2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f,D)`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\,\ell(f,x)`$ |  | (D.3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{n}(f,\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]})`$ | $`\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}\ell(f,x_{i})`$ |  | (D.4) |

With the understanding that $`S_{n}=\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}`$ are drawn
i.i.d. from $`D`$. Let
$`\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}):=\{x\to\ell(f,x):f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}\}`$
be the family of loss functions induced by
$`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$ and $`\ell`$.

We define the empirical risk minimizer (ERM) as follows.

###### Definition D.3.

(Minimizers of Population and Empirical Risk) Let $`D\in\Delta(V)`$ be
any distribution over theorems. For any $`n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}`$, suppose
$`\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}`$ are drawn i.i.d. from $`D`$. First, note that
$`f^{*}`$ is the population minimizer,

|     |                                         |     |       |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f^{*},D)=0`$ |     | (D.5) |

Now, define the ERM $`\hat{f}^{(n)}`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{f}^{(n)}\leftarrow\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}}\mathcal{L}_{n}(f,\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]})`$ |  | (D.6) |

The Rademacher complexity⁴⁴ 4 This definition is different than
[Definition 3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Definition 3.3 (Rademacher Complexity). ‣ Contrastive Learning. ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
previously defined and used in the context of \[[17](#bib.bib6)\] in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Theorems about Diffusion Similarity and Contrastive Learning ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
is defined as follows.

###### Definition D.4.

For a function class $`\mathcal{F}`$, and data distribution $`D`$, the
average Rademacher complexity is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}):=\mathbb{E}_{\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}D}\mathbb{E}_{\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\{\pm 1\}}\Big[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(x_{i})\Big]`$ |  | (D.7) |

Upper bounding the Rademacher complexity of
$`\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})`$ will upper bound the
generalization error of the ERM. In particular,

###### Lemma D.5.

(Corollary 4.19 of \[[28](#bib.bib3)\]) For any
$`\delta>0,n\in\mathbb{N}`$, let $`S_{n}:=\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}`$ be a
training set of size $`n`$ drawn i.i.d. from $`D`$, and let
$`\hat{f}^{(n)}`$ minimize the empirical loss over $`S_{n}`$ (via
[Definition D.3](#A4.Thmtheorem3 "Definition D.3. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")).
Then, with probability at least $`1-\delta`$ over the draw of $`S_{n}`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\hat{f}^{(n)},D)-\mathcal{L}(f^{*},D)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\mathcal{R}_{n}(\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}))+\sqrt{\frac{\log\frac{2}{\delta}}{2n}}`$ |  | (D.8) |

###### Proof.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\hat{f}^{(n)},D)-\mathcal{L}(f^{*},D)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}(\hat{f}^{(n)},D)-\mathcal{L}_{n}(\hat{f}^{(n)},S_{n})+\mathcal{L}_{n}(f^{*},S_{n})-\mathcal{L}(f^{*},D)`$ |  | (D.9) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}}|\mathcal{L}(f,D)-\mathcal{L}_{n}(f,\{x_{i}\})|`$ |  | (D.10) |

Then, apply Corollary 4.19 of \[[28](#bib.bib3)\]. ∎

In this context, we assume an upper bound on the Rademacher Complexity
of the function class $`\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})`$.

###### Assumption 7.

(Generalization) Given prover class $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$
assume there exists a $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$-dependent
quantity $`\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})`$ where for any
theorem distribution $`D\in\Delta(V)`$, with function class
$`\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})`$ defined as in
[Definition D.2](#A4.Thmtheorem2 "Definition D.2. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
we have:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{n}(\ell(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}))\leq\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})}{n}}`$ |  | (D.11) |

The next assumption describes under what conditions it is efficient to
find the ERM from the model class $`\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}`$, on
a size $`n`$ dataset of i.i.d. theorems from a distribution of theorems.
In particular, a necessary condition for such a procedure to find the
ERM is that each theorem in the training distribution has a proof that
can be efficiently found.

###### Assumption 8.

(Optimization) Suppose we have i.i.d. sample access to theorem
distribution $`D\in\Delta(V)`$, and for any
$`x\in\operatorname{supp}(D)`$, the proof of $`x`$ is known. Then, for
any $`n`$, it is computationally tractable to find the ERM
$`\hat{f}^{(n)}`$
([Equation D.6](#A4.E6 "In Definition D.3. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"))
of a size $`n`$ dataset drawn i.i.d. from $`D`$.

Note that in practice, we may only be able to efficiently find an
$`\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}`$-ERM, for any reasonable
$`\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}>0`$, where an $`\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}`$-ERM
is a prover $`\tilde{f}^{(n)}`$ where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{n}(\tilde{f}^{(n)},\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]})\leq\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}}\mathcal{L}_{n}(f,\{x_{i}\}_{i\in[n]})+\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}`$ |  | (D.12) |

However, the remaining analysis only requires
$`\mathcal{L}(\tilde{f}^{(n)},D)-\mathcal{L}(f^{*},D)\leq\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}+2\cdot\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}}}|\mathcal{L}(f,D)-\mathcal{L}_{n}(f,\{x_{i}\})|`$.
With
$`n=\Theta(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})}{\epsilon_{\textup{gen}}^{2}})`$
samples, we get
$`L(\tilde{f}^{(n)},D)-L(f^{*},D)\leq\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}+\epsilon_{\textup{gen}}`$
with high probability. Thus, for any reasonable desired accuracy level
$`\epsilon`$, we can set
$`\epsilon_{\textup{opt}},\epsilon_{\textup{gen}}=\epsilon/2`$, finding
the $`\epsilon_{\textup{opt}}`$-ERM with generalization gap of
$`\epsilon_{\textup{gen}}`$. The necessary sample complexity would only
increase by a factor of 4, a constant factor which we neglect. With this
understanding, we keep the current phrasing of
[Assumption 8](#Thmassumption8 "Assumption 8. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
of assuming the ERM is tractable.

### D.2 Proof of [Lemma D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Finer-Grained Assumptions). ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

We now prove the main result of this section.

See
[D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma D.1 (Finer-Grained Assumptions). ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

Since $`\forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D)`$, the proof of $`x`$ is
known, then by
[Assumption 8](#Thmassumption8 "Assumption 8. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
given $`\delta>0`$ and $`n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}`$ i.i.d. samples from $`D`$,
we can compute $`\hat{f}^{(n)}`$ via
[Equation D.6](#A4.E6 "In Definition D.3. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms").
By
[Lemma D.5](#A4.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma D.5. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
[Assumption 6](#Thmassumption6 "Assumption 6. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
and
[Assumption 7](#Thmassumption7 "Assumption 7. ‣ D.1 Statistical Learning Theory Inspired Assumptions ‣ Appendix D Justification of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
we have that with probability at least $`1-\delta`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}[1-\operatorname{succ}(x,\hat{f}^{(n)})]=L(\hat{f}^{(n)},D)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\cdot\sqrt{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})}}{\sqrt{n}}+2\sqrt{\frac{\log\frac{2}{\delta}}{2n}}`$ |  | (D.13) |

By Markov’s inequality, for any $`p\in(0,1)`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,\hat{f}^{(n)})\geq p]\geq 1-\frac{\frac{4\sqrt{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})}+2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}}}{\sqrt{n}}}{1-p}`$ |  | (D.14) |

Thus, it suffices to set $`n`$ to be
$`(\frac{4\sqrt{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})}+2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}}}{\epsilon(1-p)})^{2}\leq\Theta(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{F}_{\textup{prover}})\log\frac{1}{\delta}}{\epsilon^{2}(1-p)^{2}})`$
in order for
$`\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,\hat{f}^{(n)})\geq p]\geq 1-\epsilon`$.
∎

## Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas

See
[5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 5.3 (Large "Div"^𝑃_𝜏 implies large 𝐾^𝑝_𝜏). ‣ 5.1 Diversity Measure ‣ 5 Diversity Measure and an Improved Conjecturing Algorithm ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")

###### Proof.

For a distribution $`D\in\Delta(V)`$ and subset $`A\subset V`$, denote
$`D(A)`$ as the measure of $`A`$ under $`D`$. Since $`P`$ is the
transition matrix of a nearest-neighbor-type random walk, then for any
set $`A\subset V`$, and any distribution $`D\in\Delta(V)`$, with
$`(P^{\top})^{\tau}D`$ representing the distribution of a $`\tau`$-step
random walk according to $`P`$ initialized with $`D`$, we have

|     |                                                             |     |       |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     | $`\displaystyle((P^{\top})^{\tau}D)\,(B(A,\tau))\geq D(A)`$ |     | (E.1) |

In particular, for the set
$`A=\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\}`$, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle((P^{\top})^{\tau}D)\,(B(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\},\tau))\geq\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p]`$ |  | (E.2) |

Next, for any set $`A^{\prime}\subset V`$ and any distribution
$`D^{\prime}\in\Delta(V)`$, the cardinality of $`A^{\prime}`$ is lower
bounded in terms of its measure under $`D^{\prime}`$ and the (weighted)
two-norm of $`D^{\prime}`$. In particular, we apply
[Lemma E.1](#A5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma E.1. ‣ Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")
with $`A^{\prime}=B(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\},\tau)`$
and $`D^{\prime}=(P^{\top})^{\tau}D`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|K_{\tau}^{p}(f)|`$ | $`\displaystyle:=|B(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\},\tau)|`$ |  | (E.3) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{((P^{\top})^{\tau}D)\,(B(\{x\in V:\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p\},\tau))^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\frac{1}{||(P^{\top})^{\tau}D||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi)}}`$ |  | (E.4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim D}[\operatorname{succ}(x,f)\geq p])^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\textup{Div}^{P}_{\tau}(D)`$ |  | (By [Equation E.2](#A5.E2 "In Proof. ‣ Appendix E Auxiliary Lemmas ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms")) |

∎

###### Lemma E.1.

For graph $`G=(V,E)`$, let $`\pi:V\to(0,\infty)`$. For any distribution
$`D^{\prime}\in\Delta(V)`$ and any $`A^{\prime}\subset V`$, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|A^{\prime}|\geq\frac{(D^{\prime}(A^{\prime}))^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\frac{1}{||D^{\prime}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi))}}`$ |  | (E.5) |

###### Proof.

For any distribution $`D^{\prime}\in\Delta(V)`$, any $`\alpha\in[0,1]`$,
and any $`A^{\prime}\subset V`$, we have:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle(D^{\prime}(A^{\prime}))^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq(\sum_{x\in V}\mathbf{1}_{A^{\prime}}(x)D^{\prime}(x))^{2}`$ |  | (E.6) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq[\sum_{x\in V}(\mathbf{1}_{A^{\prime}}(x)\sqrt{\pi(x)})^{2}]\cdot[\sum_{x\in V}(D^{\prime}(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi(x)}})^{2}]`$ |  | (E.7) |

Thus,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|A^{\prime}|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in V}\mathbf{1}_{A^{\prime}}(x)`$ |  | (E.8) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{\sum_{x\in V}(\mathbf{1}_{A^{\prime}}(x)\sqrt{\pi(x)})^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}`$ |  | (E.9) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{(D^{\prime}(A^{\prime}))^{2}}{\sup_{x\in V}\pi(x)}\frac{1}{||D^{\prime}||^{2}_{\ell^{2}(1/\pi))}}`$ |  | (E.10) |

∎

###### Lemma E.2.

Let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a finite, undirected, connected, and non-bipartite
graph. Let $`(V,P)`$ be a nearest-neighbor-type Markov chain on $`G`$.
For every $`x\in V,`$ let $`N(x)`$ denote its neighbors in $`G`$. If
$`\,\forall x\in V,\forall y\in N(x),P[x,y]>0`$, then $`P`$ is
irreducible and aperiodic, and there exist constants $`C>0`$ and
$`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\max_{x\in V}||p^{(n)}(x,\cdot)-\pi||_{\textup{TV}}\leq C\alpha^{n}`$ |  | (E.11) |

###### Proof.

Because $`G`$ is connected, then
$`\forall x\in V,\forall y\in N(x),P[x,y]>0`$, so $`P`$ is irreducible.

Because $`G`$ is undirected,
$`\textup{gcd}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}\leq 2`$. Because $`G`$
is non-bipartite,
$`\textup{gcd}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}\neq 2`$. Thus, $`P`$ is
aperiodic.

Because $`V`$ is finite and the rows of $`P\in[0,1]^{|V|\times|V|}`$ sum
to $`1`$, then $`P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}`$, so that $`P`$ has an
eigenvalue of $`1`$. The left eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue
$`1`$ is the stationary distribution $`\pi`$. Since $`P`$ is
irreducible, $`\pi`$ is unique.

By
[Lemma A.3](#A1.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma A.3. ‣ Isoperimetric Inequality. ‣ A.1 Preliminaries. ‣ Appendix A Proof of ‣ A Theoretical Framework for Self-Play Theorem Proving Algorithms"),
there exist constants $`C>0`$ and $`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\max_{x\in V}||p^{(n)}(x,\cdot)-\pi||_{\textup{TV}}\leq C\alpha^{n}`$ |  | (E.12) |

∎
